en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Huayan Yuanren Lun*, composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánjué, who lectures on the sūtras and śāstras at the Great Kaiyuan Monastery in Cháng’ān.

The teachings established by the Three Sages follow divergent paths yet wondrously accord; the writings of the multitude of worthies differ according to their respective doctrines. This has led people to grasp merely at the finger [pointing to the moon].
Among those followers, they vied with one another in creating contradictions; thus, those who sought the source and investigated the root to find its ultimate purpose were truly few.

Guifeng Chan Master of the Tang Dynasty took pity on them; he therefore examined the sacred mind of both internal and external teachings and probed the profound subtleties of the "Half" and "Full" [teachings].
He composed this elegant treatise, entitled *Yuanren wen* (Inquiry into the Origin of Humanity), which opens four gates and encompasses all manner of excellence.
This shall cause them to cease their divergent views and reveal to them the true refuge, so that they need not seek elsewhere; it leads directly to awakening.

Observing its rhythmic modulation and rigorous investigation, its citations and harmonizations, its eloquence without floridity and its thoroughness without partiality—it is profound, precise, concise, and brilliant;
it deepens the small channels to block the streams and guides the rivers to pour into the sea. Truly, this is for the sake of all living beings.
This is a guide to the wondrous source. Were it not for one who is brilliant, comprehensive, and has deeply penetrated the threshold of the sages and worthies, could such a work be produced?
Prime Minister Pei once said, "The Tathāgata is the master who expounds the teachings; my teacher is the person who synthesizes those teachings.
How true these words are! Prime Minister Pei has provided this preface, and Master Lingshan Li has further inscribed this colophon at the end.
The Chan Master Wansong further opened up nine pairs and eighteen layers to praise this teaching. The Three Sages were all men who had attained the Way and did not grant their approval lightly;
unless one’s principle returned to the ultimate correctness, how could even a gentleman be partisan?

I have once examined the various commentaries on the sutras and śāstras by Guifeng, which elucidate the Chan school in over one hundred and ten volumes; among them, only those concerning the *Avataṃsaka*...
Commentaries on such works as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith* have long been prevalent in the world;

yet, I have always regretted that these texts had not been sufficiently elucidated. Previously, while in Chang’an, during my leisure from lecturing and recitation, I gathered various interpretations and composed a brief commentary.
Initially, I intended to append it to the text itself, but fearing it might become confused with the formal commentaries (*śāstra*), I have recorded it separately.

I have kept this within my book-chests for my own perusal; now that I have arrived at the capital, as students repeatedly requested it, I have again set forth its general outline at the beginning of this work.
Although the writing is crude, the meaning appears to follow a central principle.
Those who wish to know what makes us human beings must not fail to devote their attention to this book. Written on the day after the full moon of the fourth month in the year of Zhìzhì Rénxū.
Preface to the *Huayan Yuanren Lun Jie* (Exegesis on the Huayan Treatise on the Original Person), Volume One, composed by the śramaṇa Yuánjué,
who lectures on the sūtras and śāstras at the Great Kaiyuan Monastery in Cháng’ān, at the Eastern Pavilion of Wàn’ān in the Capital.

△ This treatise, when analyzed, consists of four major sections: first, the title; second, the author; third, the preface; and fourth, the main text. The explanation of the title further divides into two parts:
first, the explanation of the actual title, and second, the explanation of the title together with the preface. Now, for the first part, the explanation of the actual title.
The Avataṃsaka Treatise on the Origin of Humanity:

Regarding the two characters "Huayan" (Avataṃsaka), this refers to the sūtra that serves as its primary authority. As for the "Treatise on the Origin of Humanity," it precisely elucidates what has been composed.
The sūtra upon which it relies is fully titled the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. Master Qingliang stated: "As for 'Mahāvaipulya'..."
Regarding the Dharma that is realized, the *Avataṃsaka* is so named because within the Dharma realized by the person who realizes it, there are three greatnesses:

"Great" refers to the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*), "Vast" refers to the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*), and "Broad" refers to the greatness of function (*karma-mahattva*). Regarding the person who realizes it, there is both cause and fruit;
the *Avataṃsaka* is the cause and the Buddha is the fruit. Thus, "Flower" (*Hua*) is Samantabhadra and his myriad practices, while "Adornment" (*Yan*) is Mañjuśrī and Great Wisdom.

"Wisdom" refers to taking great wisdom as the sovereign to direct the myriad practices, thereby adorning the originally existent Dharma of the Great Vaipulya and accomplishing the fruit of the ten bodies of Vairocana Buddha;
thus, the single character "Sūtra" (Jing) signifies the teaching that expresses this meaning, which is not different from what is fully explained in the title of the original commentary.
As for why it is specifically designated within the title of the present treatise:
Because this is the primary tenet of this treatise, among the five subsequent teachings, the One Vehicle that Reveals Nature (*ekayāna-prakṛti-vyakti*) is precisely this sūtra;
thus, it is not fully cited here as it is not a direct commentary on the sūtra.

Regarding the title *Yuanren lun* (Treatise on Tracing Back the Origin): "tracing back" (*yuan*) means to investigate its fundamental source. Xu Xian’s *Shuowen Jiezi* explains: [it refers to]... [the act of tracing back].
"Original" (*yuan*) refers to the source of a spring; later generations added the radical for water to it, using it instead for "original marsh" (*yuanyí*).
This [usage] is not what is intended here. Since we wish to investigate the fundamental origin of humanity, we say "originate from man" (*yuánrén*). As for "man" (*rén*):

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that because they possess much deliberation and thought, they are called "men. Furthermore, "man" (*rén*) means that their bodies and speech are supple; moreover, "man" (*rén*) is a name.
Regarding the phrase "there is another person who possesses pride," the commentary explains that "pride" refers generally to discursive thought (*vitarka*).
This means that among human beings, mental reflections—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—are manifold and distinct from moment to moment; it is for this reason that the term is used.
The description of "gentleness of body and speech" specifically refers to virtuous persons who have overcome pride; conversely, this applies to practitioners who act otherwise.
Regarding the existence [of this state], the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Because the mind is tranquil, it is called 'human' (*manuṣya*). The commentary explains:

This distinguishes [humans] from those in the evil realms who are oppressed by manifold sufferings and lack any time of tranquility; furthermore, it is spoken of in terms of their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).

It is as the *Liji* (Book of Rites) says: "Humanity is born tranquil; this is the nature of Heaven. Question: Buddhism constantly speaks of sentient beings as encompassing the five destinies (*gati*) and so forth; why is this [the case]?

The treatise merely sets forth the "original person" (yuanren) as its response to the Master of the Treatise, who argues that the person is of the same category as the self (*ātman*). Thus, the preface states:

"Now I have obtained this human body, yet I do not know [myself]" (and so forth). Furthermore, among the six realms of existence, the other five destinies possess an uneven distribution of suffering and joy and are incapable of practicing the path;
therefore, the exhortation is directed specifically toward humans. Hence it is called the "Original Person. [This was written by] Prime Minister Pei Yuan.
The Preface to the Awakening states: That by which sentient beings come and go are the six realms of existence. Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and sorrow;
birds and beasts harbor the grief of flight and slaughter; the asuras are in the midst of rage, while the devas are in the height of pleasure.
To rectify the mind and incline toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable of this. All Buddhas of the three periods of time have [attained it] within the human realm.
This is why one attains Buddhahood within the center; the meaning of this may be verified and set forth in the subsequent text.
Once the source of humanity is known, the categories of the four sages and the six classes of ordinary beings can likewise be understood.

"Lun" (Treatise) refers to critical evaluation, wherein host and guest are provisionally established to engage in dialogue, inquiry, and thorough investigation of profound principles, thereby instructing students.

It is merely named a "Treatise" (*śāstra*); if one were to provide a comprehensive explanation, the "original source" (*yuan*) refers to the capacity [of the subject] and the "person" (*ren*) refers to the object.
This "original source of the person" (*yuan-ren*) is the basis for the treatise; the sequence of the agent, the locus, and the activity can thus be understood.

Alternatively, "the original source is the person" and "the treatise on the original source of the person"—these two interpretations are the reverse of the former. Looking back at what is taken as the fundamental principle above, it is the *Avataṃsaka*.

The *Treatise on the Original Person* (*Yuanren lun*) either adopts the title of a major scripture to serve as the heading for this treatise; thus, by taking the name of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is categorized as a "possessive compound" (*yǒucái*).
This concludes the explanation of the main title. △ Next is the explanation of the preface and the sequence [of the work].
"Along with the Preface.
"Along with" (bing) carries the meaning of inclusion; "Preface" (xu) means source or introduction.

Because it serves as the introductory thread leading into the main text that follows, the title "Treatise Along with Preface" is treated as a single unit by one person. Thus, no separate title for the preface is established; it is simply appended to the title of the treatise.
Because this follows the preceding section and is accompanied by a preface, it is written in smaller characters to distinguish it from the main text;
thus, it serves as a separate commentary on the various combinations and divisions within the general title. △ Second, the author.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi at the Guifeng Hermitage of Caotang Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
Regarding the hermitage on Mount Zhongnan, it is the specific location upon which he relied; "Mount Zhongnan" is the general name for the entire range.
Geographically belonging to the Three Qin regions, it stretches east and west for over eight hundred *li*. Within Mount Zhongnan, this particular site is distinguished from the rest.

The phrase "the old thatched hall on the mountain" (shàngù cǎotáng) specifically indicates his own dwelling; however, since a general description of the Zhōngnán region would have been too vast and diffuse, he mentions this again.
Furthermore, the Thatched Hall was originally the Xiāoyáo Garden of the Later Qín dynasty;

after Kumārajīva entered the Qín territory, an imperial decree ordered that scriptures be translated within this garden, and a thatched hall was established for him to reside in, which subsequently became a monastery (*sì*). *Sì* means "to govern" (*sī*); it is the state’s... [text ends].

The establishment of nine monasteries to correspond with the Nine Ministers originated when the monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived during the Han dynasty and were housed in the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù).
Thereafter, the residences of monks were called "sì" (monasteries), beginning with the Bǎimǎ (White Horse) Monastery in Luoyang.
As for the Guìfēng Āraṇya, Guìfēng is a secondary peak of Zhōngnán; its mountain resembles the scepter held by a king.
Guī (the name of the master) was thus named after this place. In Sanskrit it is called *araṇya*, which here means a "place of tranquility.
As a dwelling for those who have left the household life, it must be situated far away from clamor and bustle; therefore, in this land, people prefer brevity and simply call it "Lanruo" (*araṇya*).

Both the "Grass Hall Monastery" (*Càotáng sì*) and the "Lanruo of Guìfēng" are examples of the *yǒuzhǔ shì* (dependent designation) interpretation. Furthermore, the Grass Hall and Guìfēng were not far apart, as the Master himself noted.
He resided sometimes at Caotang (Grass-Hall) and sometimes at Guifeng (Crag-Peak). As the Preface by Prime Minister Pei states:
"The Master of the Treatise traveled north to Qingliangshan and upon his return resided at Caotang Temple in Hu County; not long after, he entered Guishan to the south of the temple.

For this reason, both are mentioned together. Some scholars interpret the reference to Caotang Temple as being in proximity to the Guifeng Aranya, or perhaps they consider them to be the same location.
This concludes the analysis of the *tatpuruṣa* compound—both collective and distributive—referring to the location of Zhongnan Mountain, which accords with the expectations of the commentators.
Regarding the term "śramaṇas" and so forth, these refer to the individuals who narrate [the text]. The meaning of the two characters "Śramaṇa" is explained as usual.

As for the two characters "Zongmi," they are the master’s specific name. His secular surname was He; he was a native of Xichong in Guozhou. In his youth, he studied the Confucian classics, but then encountered...
The Venerable Yuan, a descendant of the Venerable Heze, found a karmic affinity with him at Suizhou;

he subsequently received the tonsure and ordination, studied both internal and external teachings, and became thoroughly proficient in the commentaries and sub-commentaries on various sutras and treatises such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Complete Enlightenment*.
He authored the *Chan-yuan ch’üan*, which circulates in the world alongside his other works. As detailed in his own biography, the śramaṇa Zongmi esteemed him as a master of the school.

Regarding the two explanations based on the agent (*kartṛ*) and the action (*kriyā*), one may understand them as explaining the relationship between the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*)—such as the aforementioned Mount Zhongnan—in relation to the preceding [text].
The single character "narrative" (*shu*) expresses the accomplishment of the work. As the former masters said: "To describe principles is called 'narrative' (*shu*);
because it existed previously, it is called 'created' (*zao*); because it is newly initiated here, this treatise should properly be named 'created' (*zao*). This is indeed the case.

The Master of the Treatise, with his wondrous wisdom that exhausts the source of the aggregates and his vast talent for broad comprehension, has deployed the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables and inscribed them upon brushwork, ink, and tablets.
He entices those who are heterodox and deluded toward the Right Path and repels those on the peripheries toward the Great Vehicle.

Having achieved this merit, he does not boast of it, but merely says he is "expounding. Through this exposition, the functions of the capable agent and the object of explanation can be understood. Thus ends the explanation.
The author has finished [the preface].

△ From here below, the third section, the "Introductory Exposition," is divided into three parts: first, a general elucidation of the main purport; second, a specific narration of the various schools;

and third, the formal exposition of the composition of this treatise. The first part also consists of two sections: first, establishing the fundamental tenet by referring to its source; within this, there are two further divisions.
First, to accord with clarity:
the myriad spirits stir and move, yet all possess their origin; the myriad things flourish and multiply, yet each returns to its root.

As for the "myriad spirits," this includes those with feathers, fur, scales, and shells, as well as insects and other such creatures; their species are manifold, yet they all possess sentience and awareness.
Therefore it is said that the myriad spirits emerge from the state of being "chun" (dormant/stupid). The *Erya* states that "zuo" means to move.
Species such as insects hibernate during winter and move when they encounter spring; thus, their characters include the radical for "spring" (春) and the character for "insect" (虫).

In this current treatise, we provisionally cite the "chun-chong" (dormant insect) as a subtle example of movement to illustrate the human condition; in reality, this encompasses all modes of birth—oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born.
To say that "all have their basis" means that the "basis" refers to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains regarding sentient beings: "Mental karma is the cause;
the egg, womb, moisture, and transformation are the conditions; thus the five aggregates arise. The *Awakening of Mahābodhi* (*Mahābodhi-saṃbodhi*) states:
"If there are all varieties of worlds—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—they all take sexual desire as the cause for the formation of their life and nature."

One should know that craving is the root of saṃsāra. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "With a perverted mind, one approaches the realm of desire; moisture-born and transformation-born beings are defiled by odors and locations.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Egg-born beings arise solely from thought; womb-born beings are caused by emotion; moisture-born beings are produced through contact;

and transformation-born beings correspond to separation. The *Vajraśekhara-śāstra* states: "Birth is categorized according to their support: those born from a shell are called egg-born; the moving species..."

That which is contained within and emerges is called "womb-born" (*jarāyu-ja*); it belongs to the category of desire. That which arises through the reliance on moisture is called "moisture-born" (*saṃsveda-ja*);

it belongs to the category of those who proceed by means of moist contact. That which does not arise from parents but suddenly comes into being through the union of mental conceptions is called "transformation-born" (*upapāduka*);

it belongs to the category of those who respond to conditions through detachment. Transformation-born beings also arise from their own mental conceptions; they imagine a superior place and, through affection for that realm, [are reborn there].
Because they arise through transformation (*upapāduka*), it is said that they are free from the physical body;

thus we know that among the classes of sentient beings, regardless of whether they are large or small, all take defiled craving as their very foundation—this is cited here using sentient beings as an illustration.

"Ten thousand things" refers to the various categories of the hundred grains, grasses, and trees; "flourishing" describes their state of profuse growth. This passage borrows from the *Laozi*, which states:
"All things, flourishing in their abundance, return to their root. Returning to the root is called stillness;
stillness is called the restoration of the mandate (*ming*). (and so forth). The intent of that [text] is that all things are born from the Dao and return back to the Dao.
It is to restore its original root. Now, my intention is simply to take the fact that all things have their respective roots as the premise, so that only then can branches and leaves flourish;
this is citing the insentient as an example. △ Second, the reverse conclusion.
There has never been a case where there are branches and twigs without a root. The *Guǎng yùn* states:
"One [radical] beneath the wood radical signifies the 'root' (běn), referring to the rootstock; one [radical] above the wood radical signifies the 'tip' (mò), referring to the branches and leaves.
If there were no root, how could there be branches and twigs? △ Next, the actual manifestation of the object [is explained].
For example, how much more so for that which is the most intelligent among the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) yet lacks an origin?
Furthermore, it is said that by means of analogy, one clarifies above that even insects, grasses, and trees still possess causes and conditions; thus they may be compared to humans.
If one establishes oneself in this manner, how could one fail to exhaustively investigate the fundamental source? Regarding the "Three Powers" (sān cái), these are Heaven, Earth, and Humanity;

"power" (cái) refers to capability. This means that Heaven possesses the power of movement, Earth possesses the power of generation and completion, and Humanity possesses the power of discernment and reflection.
As the ancients said: "Heaven produces all things, yet only humanity is most spiritual. Since it is called "most spiritual," [it must be so].
This is that which excels all things; can it be without a foundation? △ Second, establishing the principle by tracing back to its source, in two parts:
first, establishing the principle.
Now, "to know others is wisdom; to know oneself is clarity."
These two phrases are taken entirely from the *Laozi* commentary by Emperor Minghuang, which states: "The wise employ [their minds] to know things;
the enlightened illuminate to discern the subtle. The wise know nothing they do not know; the enlightened illuminate nothing they do not perceive.

The sub-commentary explains this as follows: "Knowledge" (*zhì*) refers to investigation. It means that one employs the mind to generate wisdom and uses this wisdom to investigate the excellence of others.

How could evil be called wisdom? If one reflects inwardly and examines within, clearly observing that the mind does not give rise to the cognition of dharmas, this is what is meant by "clear understanding.
In the present text, the application of the mind does not stop at this point;

as will be shown later in the section revealing the true source, it is only when one realizes that the nature is identical to the Buddha that this constitutes the true wisdom-illumination of this school. Since the root encompasses the branches, there is likewise [no end].
It is left behind. △ Next, the correct elucidation of the two aspects of being able to trace the origin. First, the reductio ad absurdum showing the necessity of tracing the origin:
"Now that I have received this human body, if I do not know from whence it comes, how can I know where one goes in future lives?
How can I know the affairs of men throughout the past and present of the world?"
The term "I" (我) refers to the provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*) composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which the author uses to refer to himself;
by citing his own example, he seeks to exhort others. "Inherited" (*bǐng*) means to receive or be endowed with, as the *Xiaojing* states:

"The body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents," meaning that there is something inherited through which this body is obtained. "That from which it comes" refers to what was inherited in previous lives, based on internal [conditions].
The teaching explains that past karma and afflictions evolve successively until they reach the *tathatā* of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). Why is this so?
"Other worlds" refers to future lives; "destinations" (*gati*) means tending toward them—once this body has been cast off, to which realm will one be born:
the heavens or hell? Whether ascending or falling, the intent is that since one does not know from where one comes when reborn, [the nature of these transitions must be understood].
Furthermore, how can one know the destination of death? This is what is meant by the Master’s words: "If you do not yet know life, how can you know death?
Human affairs throughout the world across all time consist of horizontal constraints within the world and vertical constraints through the ages.
These human affairs include the rise and fall of dynasties, the beauty or depravity of customs, the formation or decay of ritual and music, and the administration of laws and government.
This refers to matters such as gain and loss. However, knowing where these originate and the destination one will take in future lives is the matter of "foreknowledge of oneself";
knowing the affairs of people throughout the past and present of the world is the matter of "foreknowledge of others.
Taking the self as the root and the past and present of the world as the branches, one must first investigate the root before exhausting the branches; only then will it not be so.

This is to lose their proper order. If one spends the entire day discussing the past and present of the world, yet remains ignorant of the ultimate nature of this very body, then one abandons the root to attend to the branches.
Consider Sima Qian, who compiled the *Shiji* yet could not escape severe punishment;

or Yang Xiong, who authored his treatises yet ended his life by throwing himself from the tower—can they be called men of wisdom? Thus says the *Book of Poetry*: [The original text here would follow with the relevant verse.]
"Is this not what is meant by the saying: 'To be both enlightened and wise so as to preserve one's person'? Later, he followed [the path] until he attained the essential meaning;
thus, for several decades, he studied without fixed teachers, extensively investigating both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings to trace back to his own person.
By tracing it back without ceasing, he finally attained that person."
"Learning from no fixed teacher" means that one does not take only a single person as a master. Qingliang said: "Those who benefit me are my friends; I befriend them all.
"Broad" refers to vastness, and "skillful" refers to thorough mastery. Internally, this concerns the essential tenets of the Buddhist schools;
externally, it concerns the texts of Confucianism, Daoism, and the hundred other lineages. His resolve lies in the exhaustive investigation of his own [nature].
This is not a study undertaken for the sake of emolument or fame. As the Master [Confucius] said: "The scholars of antiquity studied for themselves; the scholars of today study for others.
To investigate the source without end is "for oneself," whereas to stop is "for others. When one has not yet reached the ultimate, the mind does not cease;

once the work is accomplished, it must reach its destination. Because one attains the fundamental source, this preface to the commentary on the *Awakening of Faith* (Yuanjue) is presented as the primary discourse.

"With hair in braids, he specialized in the Confucian classics; with the capping ceremony completed, he investigated the Buddhist scriptures. He encountered Chan in the Southern Capital and met the teaching of the Perfect Ultimate.
Furthermore, it is said that "he traveled to a hundred cities on foot and sat to explore the myriad texts"—all of which refers to these very matters.
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the various schools (5): First, the exposition of non-Buddhist teachings.
Now, those who practice Confucianism and Daoism know only that, in the near term, this body was transmitted and received through the continuous succession of their ancestors;
and in the distant past, the single qi of Chaos was divided into Yin and Yang, from which the two [principles] gave rise to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
The three [powers] generate the myriad things, and both the myriad things and human beings take *qi* as their fundamental substance.

The Great Master Mingjiao (Chan Master Qisong of the Song Dynasty, author of the *Fujiao bian*, which was presented to the court; Emperor Renzong permitted its inclusion in the canon and bestowed upon him the title Great Master Mingjiao;
much of the following text cites this work) states that Daoism and Confucianism share the same source, originating from the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; therefore, we shall follow this here.

In ancient times, these were combined to clarify that Confucianism takes Confucius as its primary authority; Cheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Nanhua* (Zhuangzi) states that "Ru" is a surname, Zheng, with the given name Huan.
The *Pianyun* glossary explains that "Ru" means "gentle. As for the Way, it refers to Daoism, which takes Laozi as its primary authority;
subsequently, Lie Yukou and Zhuang Zhou both followed this tradition. Later generations, such as the followers of Zhang Ling, mixed these together.

To claim that such heterodox explanations are not the fundamental intent of Laozi, yet to say that the Way of the Teachings (Dàojiào) merely takes the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi as its ancestors and fathers—(and so forth)—is to transmit by summarizing from the root to the branches. It is to speak of continuing with the branches while taking the root as the basis;

it is to speak of the grandfather transmitting to the father, the father transmitting to the son, such that the generations do not cease. The son continues the father, the father continues the grandfather, revolving and turning in succession.
Reaching back to the most remote ancestors, the *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "The parents give birth to us; there is nothing greater than continuing their lineage.

When tracing this back further, one pushes the inquiry ever deeper until it reaches the primordial unity of the *hun-yuan* (the chaotic origin). This means that prior to Heaven and Earth, there was only the single, unified *yuan-qi* (primordial pneuma), undifferentiated and indistinct;
hence it is called "chaotic" (*hun-tun*). To "divide" (*pou*) means to separate; thus, once the chaos has been divided...
After the division, the yang-qi is light and clear, and thus ascends; the yin-qi is heavy and turbid, and thus descends. That which ascends becomes Heaven, and that which descends becomes Earth.
The two qi harmonize and unite, and humans are born within them; this constitutes the Three Powers (triple harmony). From this, the myriad things gradually come into being.
The *Daodejing* says: "The Dao gives birth to the One; the One gives birth to the Two; the Two give birth to the Three; the Three give birth to the myriad things."

Regarding "The myriad things," Emperor Ming’s commentary states: "One" refers to the pneuma of vacancy (*chongqi*). It is said that when the Dao moves and produces the wondrous pneuma of harmony (*chonghe*), it is still insufficient for the principle of generating beings;
therefore, it further produces the Yang pneuma. Since the Yang pneuma cannot produce life alone, it further produces the Yin pneuma.

Because one accumulates from the single pneuma of vacancy, it is said that "One gives birth to Two. Because two [the Yang and Yin] accumulate from the dual pneumas of Yang, it is said... [Two give birth to Three].

From the two [primordial forces] arise the three; when the Yin and Yang contain and incubate the *chongqi* (the pneuma of the profound), they harmonize, and only then do the myriad things flourish and reach completion.

Hence it is said: "The three give birth to the myriad things. Furthermore, the *Zhouyi* states: "The *Yi* possesses the Great Ultimate (*taiji*), which gives birth to the Two Polarities (*liangyi*); the Two Polarities give birth to the Four Images (*sxiang*);

the Four Images give birth to the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*); the Eight Trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune; and good fortune and misfortune give rise to great undertakings (*taiye*). Moreover, the *Gou*...
The *Mingjue* states: "The *Yi* has five stages: first is *Taiyi*, called *Taiyi* [the Great Primal], wherein the phenomena and the qi have not yet differentiated;
second is *Taichu*, the sprouting of the primal qi; third is *Taishi*, the beginning of form; fourth is *Taisu*, where form undergoes transformation and possesses substance;
fifth is *Taiji*, where form and substance are fully complete. From this, heaven, earth, and the myriad things gradually arise."
Within the prevailing discourse, the views of these two schools are combined to form a comprehensive synthesis;

although the aforementioned theories differ slightly, they all maintain that *qi* (vital energy) constitutes the primordial beginning, from which humans and the myriad things gradually emerge. Thus, the conclusion of the treatise states:
"The myriad things and human beings alike take *qi* as their fundamental basis. II. Exposition of the Inner Teaching (Buddhism).
Those who study the Buddha-dharma say only this: as for the near cause, one receives this human body by undergoing retribution in accordance with the karma created in a previous life;
as for the distant cause, that karma further proceeds from afflictions (*kleśa*) through successive stages until it reaches the *ālayavijñāna*, which serves as the fundamental basis of the body.

Although this is stated generally as "the Buddha-dharma," the intent actually refers specifically to the provisional and Hinayana teachings. "Nearby" refers downward to the teachings for humans and devas;
"farther down" refers to the next phrase, the Hinayana teachings. The *ālaya-vijñāna* refers specifically to the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) teachings.

Among these three, the preceding does not include the succeeding, while the succeeding necessarily includes the preceding. Regarding the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) in the middle, it means that afflictions furthermore arise from grasping.
Furthermore, delusion and grasping each have two types. Regarding the two types of delusion: first, the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
second, the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the two types of grasping: first, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); second, the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

This means that the five aggregates and so forth arise from a multitude of conditions and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature; yet sentient beings, failing to understand this, reckon them as real—this is called the grasping at phenomena. By...
Because one adheres to phenomena, one is unable to penetrate the principles of all mundane and supramundane matters; this is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Within these five aggregates, even "phenomena" are difficult to find, let alone a "sovereign"; yet sentient beings falsely conceptualize a real self within them, which is called the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Due to this grasping at a self, the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) arises, and worldly toil and karmic retribution flourish in competition.

Because this [process] does not cease, the fruits of suffering revolve in an endless cycle. While those of the Two Vehicles merely eliminate the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) arising from self-grasping, they have not yet severed the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) arising from the grasping at phenomena (dharmagrāha). Bodhisattvas, however, sever both types of grasping and both types of obscuration.
These two graspings and two obscurations all possess seeds within the ālayavijñāna; from these seeds, the manifest arise, giving rise to delusions and creating [karma].
When one traces karma back to its root, it is found to depend upon the *ālayavijñāna*; thus it is said, "and so forth, as explained extensively below.
△ Third, the general negation:
all [the preceding views] claim to have thoroughly exhausted the principle, yet in reality they have not.
All that has been stated above consists of the expedient and gradual teachings of the sages; it is not the ultimate definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

This general refutation is intended to prevent people from becoming attached and stagnant, and its purpose lies in censuring the person rather than disparaging the Dharma. △ Fourth, resolving objections.
However, Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni are all supreme sages who, responding to the times and adapting to things, established teachings through diverse paths;
internal and external traditions complement one another to benefit the masses.

Fearing that there may be those who raise objections as previously stated—that the primal qi, yin and yang, karma, delusion, and the transformations of consciousness are all [derived from] Confucianism...
How could that which was taught by the Most Holy Śākyamuni be rejected? Therefore, it is now explained that this is simply because students do not grasp the intent of the Sages;
how could it be the fault of Confucius, Laozi, or Śākyamuni? If so, what is the intent of the Sages? The treatise states:
"As for Confucius and Laozi... (and so forth). This summarizes the intent behind the three Sages establishing their teachings, stating that they [acted] in accordance with...

Regarding those who responded to the needs of the times during the era of Confucius and Laozi: at that time, the spiritual faculties of the people in this land were not yet mature, and they were not yet capable of hearing the teachings on cause and effect, let alone the definitive discourse on Buddha-nature.

Therefore, Confucius and Laozi first gradually guided them through benevolence, righteousness, and morality, pointing toward the primordial qi and yin-yang as the fundamental principles. It was only after forty years since the Buddha appeared in the West...
In former years, the faculties of sentient beings were not yet matured and were not yet capable of hearing the definitive meaning of Buddha-nature;

therefore, the Great Awakened One provisionally taught according to the capacities of the two vehicles and the five natures, speaking of the transformation of karmic consciousness and so forth, until forty years later he finally expounded the One Vehicle.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says: "For a long time I have kept this matter hidden and did not hasten to speak," which clearly reveals this point.
"To respond to things according to the times" means that what are called "different paths" refer to distinct routes;
this specifically indicates that because the teachings established regarding primordial qi (*yuanqi*), karma, and delusion (*huo*) differ, they are termed "different paths.

As for the phrase "inner and outer mutually supporting one another," "supporting" (*zi*) means to rely upon or to assist; it means that although the established teachings differ, they nevertheless depend upon and rely on one another.

The Way proceeds in parallel without conflict; indeed, Buddhism uses Confucianism and Daoism as the initial means for attracting beings, while Confucianism and Daoism rely on Buddhism as the final means for perfecting beings.

Just as the eyes and feet must assist one another to achieve full salvation, so too, because the spiritual capacity of China is suited to transformation through benevolence, righteousness, and morality, Confucius and Laozi employed these means to transform it.
Regarding the capacities of other regions, because they are transformed through karma and delusion, the Great Awakened One transforms sentient beings by means of karma and delusion;

since such beings are not uniform, they are called "the multitudes. △ Five: Tracing the Footsteps to Reiterate the Penetration [of the Truth], Part Two: First, a General Clarification of Expedient Means and Reality, Part One: Granting Permission.
He diligently applied himself to the myriad practices to clarify the beginning and end of cause and effect, and he thoroughly investigated the myriad dharmas to reveal their origins and developments;

although these were all the intentions of the sages, one might fear that people would say: "If the sages of the three teachings are identical in their intent to benefit sentient beings, then the three teachings should all..."
One may inquire: why is Buddhism alone singled out as the primary school here? In response, it is said:

although the three sages are identical in their intention to benefit sentient beings, they differ in the application of their provisional and ultimate teachings. Confucianism and Daoism are exclusively provisional, whereas Buddhism encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate;

we now adopt the definitive teachings of the ultimate vehicle, and thus Buddhism alone is taken as the primary school. Those who are confused about the provisional and the ultimate fail to understand this.
How could one fail to grasp the Sage’s intent? When he speaks of "exhorting the practice of the myriad deeds," "exhortation" (策) refers to inciting the myriad practitioners.

Furthermore, while the gates of practice are manifold—extending beyond the mere mention of giving and precepts to include the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, the ten wholesome actions, the five precepts, the four dhyānas, the eight samādhis, the Five Constants of Confucianism and Laozi, and the Way and its Power (Tao-de)—if one examines the text closely, all of these are contained therein.

The meaning can be seen for oneself. Regarding the beginning and end of cause and effect, Buddhism alone clarifies that cultivation of the cause is the beginning and the realization of the fruit is the end;

alternatively, it refers to the sequence of a single person’s life as beginning and end. As for the ultimate origin and finality of all phenomena (*dharmas*), this principle also applies across the three teachings.

In Confucianism and Daoism, "qi" (vital energy) is taken as the fundamental basis; in the Buddhist teaching, karma, delusion, the eight consciousnesses, and *tathatā* (suchness) are taken as the fundamental basis.

According to the differences among the schools, the details can be understood: from those who diligently practice the myriad practices according to the supreme strategy, down to those who follow the intention of the Sage even when it is merely provisional.
△ Next, the refutation: there are two teachings, the Real and the Provisional;
the Provisional teaching belongs exclusively to the Buddha, while the Buddha encompasses both the Provisional and the Real.

One should ask again: "Among the three teachings, which is provisional (*upāya*) and which is real (*tattva*)? Thus, the subsequent line says, "The two teachings... (and so forth). Regarding the terms "provisional" and "real":
"provisional" means expedient or temporary, also called "expediency" (*upāyika*). A scale-pan is called a "weight" (*quan*);

it is said to be able to measure lightness and heaviness, serving as a metaphor for the Sage’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in discerning circumstances and bestowing the Way according to the capacity of the vessel. Confucius... [text truncated]
"What you have called 'capable of being established in' but not yet 'capable of being balanced' (quan) is precisely this. 'Reality' refers to the core of a fruit, taken for its hardness;
it is also a term for that which is firm and utterly unshakable. If so, may I hear about the 'balancing' (quan) of the two teachings and the 'balancing' of Buddhism?
The answer was: "There is a difference between the hidden (ming) and the manifest (xian). The 'balancing' of the two teachings is the hidden."

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): the expedient means of Buddhism is what is called "manifest expedient means. Why is this so? The Great Master Mingjiao said: "As for expedient means, there are manifest expedient means and hidden expedient means.
Manifest expedient means refers to shallow teachings and minor paths; hidden expedient means refers to heterodox ways and other teachings. The commentary states:

"Shallow teachings" refers to the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) schools; "minor paths" refers to... [the rest of the sentence continues].

Just as the two vehicles [of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] and the human and celestial realms—these three vehicles are like the parable of the conjured city—and because these are the Buddha’s teachings given according to what is appropriate, it is said that "the provisional is revealed and the provisional is hidden.
This means that his boundless and wondrous functions arise secretly and respond mysteriously;
he may act as a teacher of heterodox paths to transform those of such types, or he may act as a master of other doctrines, employing their own teachings to...
This is for the benefit of the world, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Some observe the precepts of cattle, dogs, or deer;
some wear tattered robes and serve the sacrificial fire. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Pure Dharma Practice* says:

"I dispatched Kāśyapa to become Laozi, and I dispatched the youth Jingguang to manifest as Zhongni (Confucius). Thus, we know that both Confucius and Laozi were the profound, esoteric manifestations of the Great Awakened One.

This concludes the general clarification of the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Three Teachings. △ Next, the specific clarification of the application of the provisional and ultimate has two parts; first, the exegesis:
if one promotes the myriad practices and restrains evil while encouraging good so that all return to order, then the Three Teachings may all be followed.

One should also raise this preliminary objection: "If it is previously clarified that the teachings have both provisional and ultimate aspects, yet you take only the ultimate teaching as the primary tenet, then would not the provisional teachings all become useless?
The answer is: What kind of statement is this? Indeed, when the Sages establish their teachings, each has its proper application;
whether provisional or ultimate, they accord with what is appropriate for the capacities of beings. Therefore, this very section demonstrates the utility of the provisional teachings.
The first phrase has already been explained above. To "punish evil and encourage good" means that there is one who punishes, which is to restrain and stop;

this is precisely to cease evil and promote good. Whether it be the Three Bonds and Five Constants of Confucianism, the preservation of the female and guarding of weakness in Laozi’s teaching, or the Three Studies and Six Perfections of Buddhism—none of these fail to cause people to cease evil and promote good. This is what is generally taught.
This is what is meant by the "Great Identity of the Three Teachings. The *Book of Documents* states: "The ways of practicing goodness may differ, yet they all lead to the same governance.
I now borrow this to clarify that the teachings of the Sage are like this: Shen Nong recorded a hundred medicines which, though diverse, are identical in their power to cure disease;
Hou Ji identified a hundred grains which, though distinct, are identical in their capacity to nourish humanity. Such is the teaching of the Sage.
Though they differ, they are the same in their practice of goodness; by realizing this, one may know that those who follow them all share the same destination.
Since what they return to is identical, the conduct relied upon is likewise valid for all. Thus, by relying on Confucianism, one becomes a gentleman of perfected virtue;

by following the teachings of Laozi, one becomes a pure and tranquil Perfected Man (*zhēnrén*); and by receiving the Buddhist teachings, one departs from the three evil realms to proceed toward the human and celestial realms.
This continues until one ultimately realizes the three vehicles and perfects the two fruits. △ Next, the refutation:
when one investigates the myriad dharmas, exhausts principle, and reaches the full extent of nature to arrive at the fundamental source, only then does Buddhism provide definitive resolution.
This demonstrates the function of the True Teaching (Shijiao). One should also ask: "Since all three teachings may be followed and relied upon, why must one follow the True Teaching exclusively?
Therefore, the present rebuttal states: "By examining the myriad dharmas... (and so forth).

The general meaning is that while it was previously stated that all three teachings may be followed and practiced, this was merely to accord with the Sage’s skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting beings according to their needs once they were already established [in the path].
The person does not wish to exhaustively investigate the source and root of what constitutes a human being; rather, they wish to exhaust that very root.
To do so, nothing other than the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) can fully express it. "To investigate the myriad phenomena" and "to exhaust principle and fulfill nature":
"investigation" means to seek their origin; "exhaustion" means to reach the ultimate source; "fulfillment" means to exhaust the depths of their accumulation. The "myriad phenomena" refers to—
Regarding the phenomena of form and mind, both mundane and supramundane, there is a passage from the *Book of Changes* (*Zhou Yi*) that exhaustively investigates principle and fully realizes nature.

Its *Xici* (Appended Statements) says: "Exhausting principle and fully realizing nature, one reaches destiny. The ancient sages, in creating the *Yi*, intended thereby to accord with the principle of nature and destiny.
The commentary on this states: "Principle refers to the patterns of reason; nature refers to the capacity for realization; destiny is what is born [of these]."

When one reaches the ultimate limit of investigating principles (*li*), one exhausts their capacity; if one investigates those principles to the utmost and exhausts that capacity, then one accords with the principle of nature and destiny (*xing-ming*).

Furthermore, the Confucian tradition takes what is bestowed by Heaven as "destiny" (*ming*); since Buddhism also speaks of "principle-nature" (*li-xing*), if one borrows that phrasing to grasp the intended meaning, the underlying principle differs:
"principle" refers to the principle of the Way (*dao-li*) and "nature" refers to the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena).

Because the nature of the mind does not grasp at what is bestowed by heaven, it is not called "fate. It is said that when True Suchness (tathatā) is applied horizontally to various phenomena, it is called "principle" (li), signifying its breadth;
when it penetrates vertically through a single phenomenon, it is called "nature" (xing), signifying its depth. Yet, when residing in insentient things, it is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā);
when residing in sentient beings, it is called the "mind-nature" (cittatā), also termed "buddha-nature" (buddhadhātu), "original enlightenment" (mūlapratibodha), or the "tathāgatagarbha."
This refers precisely to what is taught in the *Xianxing jing* (Sutra on Manifesting Nature), namely that dharmas such as form and mind arise from conditions and lack a real intrinsic nature;
they are entirely *tathatā* (suchness) formed according to conditions. Therefore, these myriad dharmas all take *tathatā* as their source.
Thus, the Preface to the Master’s *Yuanjue shu* states: "The myriad dharmas are false and illusory."
Arising through the convergence of conditions, the phenomena of birth are fundamentally non-existent; all is but consciousness, and consciousness is like an illusion or a dream.
This single mind is quiescent yet aware—this is termed Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*). This is what is meant by tracing all phenomena back to their original source.
Consciousness-only (*weishi*) also states: "The ultimate meaning of these phenomena is also True Suchness (*tathatā*), for it is eternally as it is in its own nature."

This refers to the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; it is precisely this meaning. As for the statement "reaching the source," it does not mean that there is a source existing apart from the true nature itself.
Rather, because the teachings distinguish between shallow and deep levels of realization, there is the distinction of reaching or not reaching it.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The true suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā*) is the essence of the single Dharma-realm, the great universal characteristic Dharma-gate."
It is said that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished, and so forth, up to: "Because it is solely this one mind, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, the section on Establishing the Thesis states: "The Mahāyāna, in general, is explained as having two aspects:
first, phenomena (*dharma*), and second, meaning (*artha*). What is meant by 'phenomena' is the mind of all sentient beings; this mind encompasses all that is mundane and supramundane."
Because the provisional teachings rely upon this mind to manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna, Master Mingjiao said:
"Whether one is a human, a deva, or a sage, who does not emerge from the self-nature? That by which they emerge is surely their fundamental basis;
this basis is the great root of all dharmas. The commentary states: "Humans, devas, and Buddhas—these three vehicles..."
If one knows that all sages emerge from this single nature, then one will understand that nature is the fundamental source of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asks: "How can the aggregates (*skandhas*) be spoken of? What is the nature of the aggregates? It states:

"The nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished; therefore, they are said to be unborn. When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent; because it is empty," [it is unborn].
That which cannot be extinguished is the meaning of non-arising. Since sentient beings are thus, so too are all Buddhas.

Since the Buddha and the dharmas of the Buddhas have no self-nature whatsoever, one knows that the wondrous nature of True Suchness—neither arising nor ceasing—is truly the fundamental source of all phenomena.
Were it not for the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle, how could this be reached? These words are decisive and conclusive.

This means that it is definitively established in its ultimate sense (*nītārtha*) and clearly elucidated; this statement specifically indicates that the Buddha’s teaching reveals the nature (*prakṛti*).
△ Third, the threefold explanation of the composition of the treatise: first, generally revealing the reasons for composing the treatise because other schools have not yet understood.
Third, the initial general clarification.
Now, contemporary scholars each adhere to a single school.
Here, "scholars" (xueshi) refers broadly to those who study the three teachings; "scholars" (shi) refers to persons, and they each adhere to one school.

That is to say, those who study Confucianism cling only to the "Mandate of Heaven," while those who study Laozi cling only to "Spontaneity" (*ziran*), and so forth, no longer investigating extensively or attaining comprehensive mastery. △ Next, to explain specifically:
even among those who take the Buddha as their teacher, they still remain deluded regarding the true meaning.

Some cling to karma and afflictions, while others cling to the transformations of consciousness; they do not believe in the true teaching of the One Vehicle. Even when discussing Buddha-nature, they invariably exclude the icchantika;
and though they speak of True Suchness, they merely describe it as unchanging. Because there is something they have not yet awakened to, it is said that they remain deluded.
This is like a group of blind men feeling an elephant: how could they know the elephant’s entire body? It is like looking at the sky from within a well: how could one see the whole of heaven?
...its boundlessness. △ Next, the conclusion and reprimand:
Thus, regarding heaven, earth, people, and things, one cannot trace them back to their ultimate source.
Question: What is the difference between this section and the previous exclusion of various schools? Answer: The previous [section] was based on what those under training know.
Regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Exoteric Teachings, the present treatise takes the attachments held by students as its starting point for composition;
had students been free from such biased attachments, the Master could have remained silent. △ Second, the actual exposition of the treatise, which is divided into three parts:
first, a preliminary account of the sources relied upon.
I shall now once again rely upon the principles of both internal and external teachings to investigate the myriad dharmas.

"I" (yu) refers to myself, the author, using this as a term of self-reference. By relying on the principles of both internal and external teachings, my understanding becomes comprehensive and harmonious, free from the defect of partiality;
it is unlike those who, having never read Buddhist scriptures, would nonetheless venture to criticize Buddhism.

"The distance between these two is vast. When the Master said, "There are those who compose works without knowing [the truth], but I am not one of them," was this not a description of the Proponent? △ Next, the specific demonstration.
Initially, proceeding from the shallow to the profound, for those who practice the provisional teachings, one dispels stagnation to ensure penetration and reaches their ultimate basis;
subsequently, relying on the definitive teachings, one reveals the meaning of successive arising, harmonizing the partial to make it perfect and reaching the "end" (the end being heaven,
earth, people, and things).
The phrase "proceeding from the shallow to the deep" refers to the first two gates of the treatise, which refute deluded attachments that are biased and superficial.
Within these, the former is shallower while the latter is deeper; this refutes stagnation to bring about penetration, thereby shattering clinging sentiments to reveal perfect understanding.
"Reaching the ultimate source" refers to the third gate, which reveals the true origin. "Ultimate" (ji) means "to reach" (zhi).

Regarding the subsequent reliance on the *nītārtha* (definitive teaching), the phrase "immediately following" refers to the fourth section, which demonstrates the successive [realizations] and so forth.

This means that within the fourth section, by employing the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) that reveals the nature, one reconciles what was previously refuted with the single ultimate truth. △ Finally, the conclusion of the names.
The text consists of four sections titled "Explaining the Origin of Humanity" (*Yuánrén*).
This may be understood.
△ The fourth major section, "Explaining the Main Text," is divided into two parts: first, the headings and enumeration of the chapters.
1. Refuting Deluded Attachments; 2. Refuting Partiality and Superficiality;
3. Directly Revealing the True Source; 4. Harmonizing the Fundamental and the Branches.
The sequence of these four sections is as previously explained. II. The Main Explanation, in four parts: first, explaining the initial chapter; second, [explaining the subsequent chapters].

Second, the refutation of partiality and shallowness; third, the explanation of the direct manifestation of the true source; fourth, the explanation of the reconciliation of the fundamental and the derivative.
Within the first [of these four], there are further two parts: first, citing the name of the gate.
First, the refutation of deluded attachments (referring to those who practice Confucianism).
"Refutation" (*chì*) means to exclude or cast out; according to the *Yǔnyùn*, it means to pursue away or distance. It signifies driving someone away until they are far removed.

"Delusion" (*mí*) refers to being confused and failing to awaken; "attachment" (*zhí*) refers to holding fast and refusing to change. △ The following two sections, "Confucianism and Daoism," specifically point [to these errors].

Regarding the Confucian and Daoist [traditions], there are three points of convergence; the fourth section, "Resolving Difficulties," clarifies what has not yet been resolved. The text of the following chapter is divided into three sections:
first, a formal elucidation of the fundamental source; second, a combined examination of the two schools.
The two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism maintain that all categories of beings, including humans and animals, are generated and nurtured by the Great Way of Non-being (xūwú dàodào).
When these two schools are compared, their meanings are as previously explained, with slight differences which shall be demonstrated according to the texts.
To say that all are generated and nurtured by the Great Way is the intention of the Master of Laozi; as the *Daodejing* states: "There was something undifferentiated and complete, existing before..."
Heaven and Earth give birth to the silent and vast, standing alone and unchanging, circulating everywhere without exhaustion;
it can serve as the mother of all under heaven. I do not know its name; it is called the Way (*Dào*).

Forcing a name upon it, I call it the Greatly Enlightened Sovereign (*Dàmíng Huáng*) to express its virtue through its capacity for universal generation, and I name it the Way to indicate its substance through its capacity for total inclusion.
Thus, she is called the Great Mother (*Mahāmātṛ*); this takes its meaning from her role as progenitor.

The intent of the Master of the Old [Laozi] is that I see a single entity formed in a state of chaotic unity, emerging from antiquity, neither sound nor color, standing forth preeminent and unshaken by shifting objects;
it dwells peacefully and expansively amidst all things, and from it all wonders emerge—it is fitting that it be so.
It is the mother of all things; therefore, a name was forcibly established for it, calling it the "Great Way" (*Daodao*).

Furthermore, the *Dejing* (Chapter on Virtue) states: "The Way gives birth to them; Virtue nurtures them; things give them form; and circumstances bring them to completion. The commentary on this passage says: "The Way descends as the harmonious and vitalizing breath (*chonghe zhi qi*) to mold and refine the myriad things;
the myriad things obtain this and are thereby born; thus it is said, 'The Way gives birth to them. Virtue is the capacity to nurture (*xiu*)."

"Nurturing" means that when the myriad things obtain the function of the Dao and are able to nourish these forms, they receive the name of "Virtue" (De) based on the place where they are nurtured by the Dao;
therefore it is said, "Virtue nurtures. The Dao gives birth to Virtue, and Virtue nurtures the myriad things so that their forms flow forth;
thus it is said, "The forms of things. The Dao acts as heaven and earth for the myriad things, providing the conditions of time, the advantages of location, and the forces of Yin and Yang.
Because material things are brought to completion through it, it is called "the completion of power" (*shìchéng*). Furthermore, it says:

"Therefore, the Dao gives birth to them, nurtures them, grows them, raises them, completes them, ripens them, nourishes them, and covers them. The commentary on this states: "To initiate [them] is 'giving birth';

to nourish [them] is 'nurturing'; to cause them to advance is 'growing'; to caress and comfort them is 'raising'; to assist and harmonize them is 'completing'; and to bring them to their ultimate conclusion is 'ripening'."

"To mature and provide for" is called "nurturing" (*yang*); "to shelter and protect" is called "covering" (*fu*). These eight characters above all refer to the functional efficacy of the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*).
△ Second, clarifying the sequence of their arising.

It is said that the Way (Dào) follows its own nature (*zìrán*), from which the primal qi (*yuánqì*) is produced; the primal qi produces heaven and earth, and heaven and earth produce the myriad things.

The single phrase "The Way follows its own nature" constitutes the entirety of the *Dàodé jīng*. It states: "Man models himself on Earth; Earth models itself on Heaven; Heaven models itself on the Way;
the Way models itself on its own nature. The commentary notes: "Man refers to the sovereign. One who would be a sovereign must first model himself on Earth."
Once tranquility is thus established, one must further emulate Heaven in its operation of generation and completion.

Once generation and completion have been achieved, one must further emulate the Dao in its purity and non-action (*wuwei*), allowing things to transform themselves. If a ruler can act in this way, he accords with the Dao and the nature of spontaneity (*ziran*).
Furthermore, it is said that "spontaneity" is the nature of the wondrous foundation; because this nature is not something produced through artificial effort, it is called "self-so."

However, "the Way" (Dao) refers to the function of the wondrous Origin; it is a designation for the relationship between the essence and its function with respect to spontaneity (*ziran*), not to say that the principles of the Way imitate spontaneity.
Now, regarding the phrase "the Way's principle conforms to spontaneity" discussed here, we do not adopt the sense of a sovereign ruler following a model;
rather, we simply clarify that the Way of spontaneity exists prior to heaven and earth. I fear...
In order to ascertain the source, I have cited these words in full: "That which is born from the primal qi" (*yuánqì*) takes its meaning from the *Dàodé jīng*.

That *Dēngjīng* states: "The Dao gives birth to the One; the One gives birth to the Two; the Two give birth to the Three; the Three give birth to the myriad things. This has already been cited in the preceding preface.
However, what is here discussed regarding "being born from the primal qi" corresponds to that "the Dao gives birth to the One," wherein the primal qi gives birth to heaven.

"Earth" refers to that which "one gives birth to two, and two give birth to three," whereby heaven and earth produce the myriad things; this corresponds to the statement that "three give birth to the myriad things.
It is merely a variation in the phrasing to emphasize novelty, yet the underlying meaning remains the same.

In the preceding narrative, "chaos" (*hundun*) represents the doctrine of the Confucianists, while here "the Great Way" (*daodao*) expresses the intent of Laozi; thus, the two are cited alternately throughout.
