If that were the case, the five virtues and six arts should also be understood of themselves without depending on practice or reflection. Why is it not so?

As for the "five virtues," they refer to the five constant virtues beginning with benevolence (*ren*), or alternatively, to the father’s righteousness, the mother’s kindness, the elder brother’s friendship, the younger brother’s respect, and the son’s filial piety.
The six arts refer to ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics. Yet, from birth, humans instinctively know how to suckle and cry;

this is due to the power of habitual practice since beginningless time, arising simultaneously with the mind. As previously mentioned, that oxen do not gore with their horns and turtles do not enter fire are all matters of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
How could it be that the primal pneuma (*yuánqì*) causes them to be so? △ Second, the extinction of the pneuma.
There should be no difficulty regarding ghosts and spirits. Part one: presenting the objection; part two: establishing the premise.
Furthermore, if birth is the sudden existence resulting from receiving vital energy (*qi*), and death is the sudden non-existence resulting from the dispersal of that energy, [then...]
△ Next is the formal objection:
"Then who would be a ghost or spirit?
Since Confucianists all maintain that the gathering of qi constitutes life and the dispersal of qi constitutes death, the present objection states: "If that is so, then as for qi..."

If [the self] were to disperse, cease, and perish, there would be no ghosts or spirits; yet the doctrine of ghosts and spirits is permitted by the Confucian school, so he uses what they acknowledge to challenge him.
However, according to the instructions of the Confucian classics, "spirit" (*shen*) means extension, and "ghost" (*gui*) means returning.

The yang-soul is called a spirit, and the yin-essence is called a ghost. Nevertheless, the *Lunyu* states: "The Master did not speak of strange anomalies, military force, disorder, or spirits. This is because...

Because the principles of ghosts and spirits are profound and obscure while the wisdom of ordinary people is shallow, one merely instructs them to revere and keep their distance, fearing that they might give rise to confusion and attachment;
yet how could this mean that ghosts and spirits do not exist? The *I Ching* says, "The refined essence forms things; the wandering soul undergoes transformation.
Thus we know the nature and appearance of ghosts and spirits: they are formed from the union of the essences of men and women, resulting in the hundred bones and four limbs.
It is said that "refined qi forms things," while the phrase "wandering souls undergo transformation" refers to what is taught in Buddhism:
because consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) is devoid of material obstruction and can move spontaneously, it is called a "wandering soul.
The meaning is that when the wandering soul unites with refined qi, it becomes a human being; when the refined qi perishes while the wandering soul does not, it becomes a ghost or spirit. If...
Within the three grades and nine classes taught in our own teachings, those possessing merit are called spirits (*deva*) and those lacking merit are called ghosts (*preta*);
though they differ in degree of excellence, both are subsumed within the realm of ghosts (*pretayoni*). △ Second, citing evidence to establish the point, in two parts:
first, citing the knowledge of past lives to prove that [the deceased] do not merely inherit vital breath (*qi*).

Furthermore, there are those in the world who possess the power of insight into past lives and can recall former events; through this, we know that the continuity of existence prior to birth is not something that suddenly arises from the mere reception of vital breath (*qi*).

Regarding those who possess such insight into past lives, for example, there was Yang Hu (style name Shuzi) of the Jin dynasty, who recognized a golden ring [as a child]. (Yang Hu, style name Shuzi, was a youth...)

Once, [Li] Hu led his wet nurse to the exterior of the Li family gate, where he found a gold ring inside a hollow in a *shuh* tree. He said to the wet nurse, "This was hidden by my ancestor when he was a child of the Li family for play.

He died at the age of seven after falling into a well; this account is from his original biography. Regarding the *Mozhi* (Inscribed Record) concerning Cui Xian’s induction: Cui Xian’s father, Rui, served as an official under Li Baozhen, the Regional Inspector of Zhe and Lu.

There was a guest named Old Man Lu who claimed to have studied the Dao under Master Mr. Li at Yunji Temple during the Sui dynasty. He frequently traveled between Yunji and Zhe-Lu, and Rui always treated him with kindness. At the end, the old man said to Rui, "I shall become a son to your family," pointing to a black mole beside his mouth.

To verify this and demonstrate that the resulting fruit was exactly as he had said, it appears in his original biography. Fang Guan opened the letter beneath the pine tree (Fang Guan, courtesy name Cili, served as the Magistrate of Tonglu during the Kaiyuan era.

Once, while passing through Xiakou with the Daoist Xing Hezhuo, they entered an abandoned temple and sat beneath an ancient pine. Hezhuo ordered someone to dig into the ground, where they discovered a jar containing letters from Lou Sided addressed to Master Yong.

Laughing, he asked Guan, "Do you remember this? Guan was suddenly enlightened, realizing his former life as Master Yong. This account is found in the *Miscellaneous Records of the Minghuang Emperor*. Su Shi composed a poem which says: "With earnest care beneath the ancient pine, he opened the letter within the jar.")

Tang Shao Stabbed the Dog Before the Lamp Tang Shao was a Grand Secretary during the Kaiyuan era who had been on good terms with Li Miao, a General of the Household living across the street from him; he treated Li with great generosity. His wife once admonished him, saying, "Do not befriend those of a different class.

Shao replied, "This is not something you understand. Later, during military maneuvers at Mount Li, Shao acted as the Minister of Rites. When Emperor Xuanzong took up the drumstick and struck the drum, less than three rounds had passed when Zhang Yue suddenly ordered Shao to announce that the Divine Martial Emperor was enraged.

The Emperor then dragged Minister of War Guo Yuanzhen down beneath the military standard, intending to execute him. Zhang Yue knelt and petitioned that Yuanzhen had meritorious service for the state and should be spared from death; consequently, Shao was executed instead. This occurred one day prior [to the execution of Guo Yuanzhen].

Shao said to his wife, "In my previous life, I was a woman of the Du family who married the son of the Wang family of Baling. At the age of seventeen, while I was threading a needle by lamplight, I fell into a deep sleep. A dog entered the room and touched the oil, soiling my clothes.

In my anger, I used scissors to stab the dog; I cut off one leg, which broke, yet the dog remained alive. I then changed the position and cut another leg, and only then did the dog die. I died at nineteen. That dog is none other than this Li Mao. Tomorrow he shall be executed. The next day it was indeed as she had said:

the first stroke of the blade did not sever the head, but upon changing the position for a second stroke, the head finally fell. (From Li Jifu’s *Record of Strange Tales*) Yuan Guan’s Old Appointment in the Gorges (from the Tang Dynasty, Li...)

Zhang Zheng’s son, Yuanlao, was on friendly terms with the Daoist practitioner Yuanguan. They had made an appointment to travel together from the Gorges into Shu. On the road, they encountered a woman washing silk. Yuanguan said to Yuanlao, "This is the place where I shall entrust myself.

He continued, "Since karmic conditions cannot be escaped, next year on such-and-such a day, you may come to visit me from Shu; let a smile serve as my token of recognition. He further remarked, "I have already been a bhikṣu for three lifetimes," and so forth. Subsequently, Yuanguan indeed died.

The following year, Yuanlao arrived at the woman's house according to the appointed time; the child had already been born for three days. Yuanlao had someone hold the infant up to the bright eaves, and the child indeed smiled. Twelve years later, Yuanlao was at Gushan under the moonlight when he heard someone tapping a cow horn and singing: "The Stone of Three Lifetimes."

The spirits of former worthies enjoy the moon and chant in the breeze—this need not be discussed; rather, let us consider how a lover of poetry has come from afar to visit. Though this physical body differs, the nature [of our minds] remains constant. (Based on the *Yeyuhua Yin*). Regarding Dongpo’s dream-tour of Shanyou:

Su Ziyu was exiled to Nan’an, where he befriended Yun’an and the Chan Master Cong. One night, Yun’an dreamed that he and Ziyu, along with Master Cong, went out of the city to welcome the Chan Master Wuzu Jie.

The next day, he told Ziyu of the dream before it had even concluded when Master Cong arrived. He related the dream exactly as Yun’an had described it. While the three were still conversing and laughing, a letter arrived from Dongpo stating: "I have already reached Fengxin; you may expect me there in a few days."

When the three met, they were greatly delighted and together traveled twenty *li* outside the city to Jian’an Temple, where Dongpo also arrived. They recounted their dreams to one another; Dongpo said, "When I was seven or eight years old, I once dreamed that I had become a monk traveling through the region of Shǎnyòu.

Furthermore, when my late mother was pregnant with me, she dreamed of a monk seeking lodging who was tall and missing one eye. Yún’ān was startled and said, "The Master Jì was a native of Shǎnyòu; he later lost an eye and, in his later years, left Wǔzǔ to travel to Nán’ān, where he passed away at Dàyú.

Counting back fifty years from now, it coincides exactly with your age—Dongpo was then forty-nine. (Excerpted from *Lěngzāi yèhuà*). Lú Nǚ recalled the long-standing grievance of her former life as a sheep-seller.

Formerly, at the house of Lu Shulun south of the city wall in Chang’an, a young woman encountered a monk begging for food between the mulberry groves. When asked where he could obtain a meal, the girl said, "Two li east of the village, at the Wang family, they are providing a vegetarian feast for monks.

She then went there and indeed found the midday meal. When the Wangs asked the monk where he had come from, the monk told them the truth. Shortly thereafter, the Wangs’ elderly parents arrived at the girl’s house. The girl closed her door and would not come out. Her mother asked her, "No one knows that my family has set up a vegetarian feast; how did you know?

The girl emerged from her room and called out, "On such-and-such a day and month, where are the father and son, the Hui merchants who trade in sheep? The old couple hurried out in alarm. The mother asked the girl, "Why were you acting like this just now? The girl replied, "In a previous life, I was a Hui merchant from Xiazhou who traded in sheep."

I stayed at his house; he killed my father and son and took all our sheep as his own. Later, I became his son. At fifteen, I fell ill, and at twenty, I died. Although the expenses for medicine and treatment already exceeded what he had extorted from me, he continued to provide me with offerings for the *zhāi* (memorial services) every year.

Nevertheless, the debt of one's life must still be repaid. (*Chūyìshǐ*) Xishan Resolves the Doubtful Case of Patricide: During the early years of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty, when Zhen Xishan was the Regional Inspector of Changsha, there were two citizens named Cheng Er and [the second name lost].

One of them had a son aged twenty who plotted to murder his father. He spoke secretly to a friend, fearing that if the matter leaked out, they would both be implicated. Consequently, the friend reported it to the authorities. The authorities immediately summoned the son to question him, and the son did not deny it. (*Yìtǔ*)

When he questioned his father and the neighbors, none knew the reason; when he questioned his son regarding the plot to murder his father, there was likewise nothing he could say. Zhen then scrutinized the matter, which remained obscure, so he bathed and purified himself to offer prayers.

One night, he dreamed that a person told him, "If you simply ask your father what he did twenty years ago, you will know at once. The following day, Zhen privately asked his father, "I already know about this matter; you need only not conceal it. What did you do twenty years ago?

His father replied, "Twenty years ago, there was a practitioner from Mount Gui who wished to buy a *du-ji* (ordination certificate) for one thousand strings of cash. In the middle of the night, I killed the practitioner and buried him beneath the kitchen stove, using the money to establish a business estate. Zhen then...

I questioned his son, saying, "I wish to release you and bestow upon you one thousand strings of cash (*mǐn*) to take wherever you please. Once you have received this money, what will you do? The son replied, "If it is truly as you say, I shall purchase a *duòjié* (ordination certificate) and enter Mount Huì to become a monk. Zhenzhixing then took revenge upon his father;

he calculated his father’s estate at one thousand strings of cash, gave it to the son, and had his father exiled five hundred *lǐ* away. (From the *Jīngāng Hú Jiāngchén Jìwén*). Cases such as these are indeed numerous throughout past and present.
By verifying them through these examples, one knows that when one body is cast off and another is received, the continuity proceeds from its own kind.

It is not a matter of inheriting vital breath. △ Second, citing that ghosts possess cognition as proof that [consciousness] is not annihilated: First, refuting [the opponent's view] solely on the basis of principle and valid cognition.

Furthermore, by verifying that the spiritual cognition of ghosts and spirits is uninterrupted, one knows that after death it is not the case that the vital breath disperses and suddenly ceases to exist.

Generally speaking, those referred to as ghosts and spirits are mostly ancient sages and worthy predecessors, loyal ministers and righteous scholars whose achievements have flowed down to later generations and whose benevolence has benefited the people;
they are upright and selfless, their heroic spirits remaining unclouded. Some preside over mountains, rivers, altars of land and grain, or the state;

others administer blessings for the virtuous and calamities for the lewd. They are honored by the state through the rites of the sacrificial canon, and the people find fulfillment in their prayers and supplications. This is what is meant.
As for their presiding deities, there are wood-spirits, mountain-essences, powerful souls, and malevolent ghosts;

some take advantage of a person’s decline or exhaustion, while others attach themselves to objects to communicate. They cause fear among the common people and seek offerings and prayers—this is called "licentious sacrifice.
Although the orthodox and the heterodox differ, they both possess spiritual awareness. If one were to claim that the vital energy dissipates upon death, then as for these spirits...
For what reason? It can be well corroborated by the fact that many poems and lyrics of ghost-spirits (gui-xian) are recorded in the Collected Works of Dongpo (Sūn Qī).
△ Second, refuting [the opponent's position] by citing scriptures and facts, in two parts: first, refuting by citing scriptures.
Therefore, there are textual records in the classics concerning the seeking of blessings through sacrifices and prayers.
To say that there are textual records in the classics means citing the teachings to refute [the opposing view], as stated in the "Jintong" (The Golden Casket) chapter of the Book of Documents:
when King Wu was ill, the Duke of Zhou composed a memorial to pray to King Da Wang, King Wang Ji, and King Wen, requesting to offer his own person in their stead.
"I, your great-great-grandson [Name], have been struck by a violent and malignant illness (‘gou’ means to encounter; it signifies that I have encountered this sudden disease).
If you three kings—namely, King Da Wang, King Wang Ji, and King Wen—have a great responsibility toward Heaven for this son, then let Dan take the place of [Name]'s person," and so forth.
When the Duke returned, he placed the written petition inside the casket bound with golden cords.

On the following day, he recovered (after the prayers and divinations had yielded auspicious results, King Wu indeed grew better). Furthermore, the *Liji*—specifically the *Jifa*, *Jiyi*, *Jitong*, and *Liyun*—all speak of the matters of sacrifice and prayer.
Moreover, Cai Yong’s commentary on the *Yueling* states: "In the middle term of the ninth month, the sun is in the constellation Di;
[the ruler] orders the officials to collect fodder to nourish the sacrificial victims, providing them for the Great Heaven and the August Sovereign."

"Such texts as those concerning the spirits of famous mountains and great rivers in the four directions, and the offerings made to the numinous powers of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain to pray for blessings upon the people, all belong to this category.
[This section] subsequently cites events to refute [the claim].

How much more so for those who have died and returned to life, recounting the affairs of the netherworld, or who, after death, moved their wives and children to seek vengeance for grievances or repay kindness—such instances exist throughout both ancient and modern times.

Since accounts of the netherworld are largely related in the Buddhist scriptures, I fear that Confucian scholars may not yet believe them; therefore, I shall now cite examples from the Confucian tradition.

This is recorded in the *Yunyu Yangqiu* (The Spring and Autumn of Rhymed Prose), composed by Ge Liping (style name Changzhi), the former Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel during the Song dynasty.
It states that Ouyang Yongshu (Ouyang Xiu) had long been a non-believer regarding the teachings of Śākyamuni.

Once, while serving in the two highest government offices, he fell gravely ill and dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where ten men were seated in a circle, wearing ceremonial caps and robes. One of them said:

The Minister said, "How could you have come this far? You should quickly return to your lodgings. He stepped out several paces and went back to ask again, saying, "Are you not what the Buddhists call the Ten Kings?

They replied, "Indeed. He then asked, "If people of the world provide meals for monks and commission the production of scriptures to cultivate merit on behalf of the deceased, will it truly bring benefit? They answered, "How could it not be beneficial? Having said this, they woke up.
When one’s illness has finally been cured, it is like the accounts of Cui Ziyu presiding over the affairs of the Netherworld,
Han Qintu serving as King Yama, Master Yu acting as the Buddha of Rebirth, and Prime Minister Xi appearing as the Spirit of Pichang—

all of which serve as testimony to matters of the dark paths that move even wives and children, leading them to seek vengeance for grievances or repay kindnesses, as recorded in the *Zuo Zhuan* concerning Duke Xuan.
In the fifteenth year of Duke Gong, Wei Ke, a high official of Jin, had a father named Wu Zi who possessed a favorite concubine.

When Wu Zi fell ill, he said to Ke, "You must marry her off. Once his illness became critical, he then ordered that she be sacrificed as a funerary attendant. After Wu Zi died, Ke married her off, though his kinsmen opposed this.

Ke replied, "I am following my father’s valid testament" (*zhì mìng*—meaning when the illness was not yet severe; when it became severe, the mind becomes deranged and speech confused). Later, Ke... [engaged in battle].
The Qin general Du Hui was fighting at Fushi when he encountered an old man who bound the grass together to block his path;
Du Hui stumbled and fell, and [the man] captured him (Du Hui fell from his horse and was taken alive). That night, he dreamed of the old man, who said: "I am the father of the woman you married.
You followed the dying instructions of my predecessor, and I have repaid you for this. Furthermore, in the tenth year of Duke Cheng, during the reign of Jin Jing Gong...
The Duke was ill and dreamed of a Great厉 (a *lì*, meaning a great ghost) with hair reaching the ground, who beat his breast and leaped about, saying:

"You have killed my grandson unrighteously; I have obtained a petition from the Emperor. On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the sixth month, the Duke passed away. (Previously, in the second year, Lord Jing of Jin had executed the ministers Zhao Tong and Zhao Kuo without cause.

The mention of the "Emperor" refers to the Ten Kings of the Netherworld; this is because the matter concerned the path to the underworld. Furthermore, the *Jianghu Jiwen* records that during the Southern Song, Wei...
Zheng Chaoyi of this province had a grandson named [Name], who from childhood was broad-minded and capable in literature. He married a daughter of the Lu family of Kuaiji;
she too was graceful and bright. Their marital affection was profound, and Zheng once said to his wife, "Should misfortune befall us, you must not remarry;
if you should pass away before me, I shall do the same. His wife replied, "We must indeed be equal in this."
How could eyebrows be such an ill omen? Thus they lived together for ten years, producing two sons and one daughter.
When Zheng fell ill and was on the verge of death, she finally removed her mourning dress; Lady Lu took all her assets and went to Suzhou to marry Master Zeng Cao.

Only seven days had passed since the wedding when Master Zeng received an imperial decree to examine candidates in another prefecture. While he was traveling there for two nights, Lady Lu took an evening stroll.
Between the screens of the hall, a messenger hurriedly called out from the courtyard, saying, "A letter for Master Zheng. The maid was sent to fetch it;
upon examining the outer title, she saw only the three characters "To the Lu Family," and the calligraphy was unmistakably the hand of her late husband.
When the messenger had vanished, she opened the seal and read the message, which said: "For ten years we have been husband and wife, bound by our hair."
For a lifetime you were the master of sacrifices, sharing joy from morning until night; with surplus stipends, we gathered together. Suddenly, through a great illusion, you departed for eternity.
Whom do you admire that you gave your word so lightly? You abandoned my fields and paddies and diverted our wealth to establish a separate household.
You show no concern for me having a son, nor do you think of me having a father; your righteousness is insufficient.
"As a wife, I lacked compassion; as a mother, I failed my duty. I appeal this to the High Heaven and submit my conduct to judgment in the netherworld.
Lady Lu lamented for three days and passed away. Her son, Dian, who was a court official, obtained this letter.
Part Three: Tracing the Footsteps to Resolve Objections. Section One: Setting forth the objection.
The opponent objects: "If it is the case that when a person dies they become a ghost, then since ancient times ghosts must have filled the streets and alleys;
surely there ought to be those who see them.
Why is this not so? When the outsider hears it said that people become ghosts after death, he assumes that every single person who has died has entirely become a ghost.
Knowing that there are the six realms of rebirth through which one undergoes subsequent bodies, one raises this objection: "If there are those who actually see [ghosts], why is it not so?
This question is posed in the treatise as a hypothetical inquiry from the perspective of one who does not believe in ghosts; thus it is addressed in this manner for now.
In reality, accounts of seeing ghosts have existed throughout both ancient and modern times, though they cannot be cited in full here. △ Subsequently, the general explanation follows.
The answer is: When humans die, they do not necessarily all become ghosts; when ghosts die, they may again become humans and so forth.
How could it be that ghosts accumulated since antiquity exist eternally?
To say that "humans die and go to the six realms" means that some may be born in heaven, some may return as humans, or some may become birds or beasts.
Regarding those who fall into hell, the aforementioned "hungry ghosts" (preta) refer merely to a single realm of existence.

As for the statement that a ghost may again become a human, this means that once the karma of being a ghost has been exhausted, one may either become a human or transmigrate into another realm. How could this ancient [text] be criticized as being as inflexible as a fixed peg?
According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan), during the Jianhe era of the Later Han dynasty, the śramaṇa An Shigao was traveling by boat.
Upon arriving at the shores of Hongting Lake, there was a shrine to the lake deity. The deity descended and said, "The śramaṇa on the boat was my spiritual companion in a previous life;
please bring him here to rest within the shrine. Once he had arrived, the deity wept and pleaded, "I and you were once fellow practitioners of the Way.
Because of my anger, I fell into this realm; I pray that you will have pity on me and save me."
The Master requested that his true form be manifested, and the deity said, "My true form is hideous; I fear it might startle you. Anan replied, "Have no concern.
Suddenly, a great python emerged from behind the bed and extended its head toward Anan. Anan comforted it by preaching the Dharma and transforming it through the language of India.
The python wept and thanked him, saying, "Fortunately, I have heard your teaching; now I am liberated from suffering. [He then offered] a thousand rolls of silk.
He provided An with the materials—some yellow and some white silk—to perform meritorious deeds on his behalf.

An then established a monastery in Yuzhang (the *Yeyu* states that this is the present-day Dà'ān Monastery in Hóngzhōu). Shortly thereafter, a large python was seen dead in the marshy grasses behind the mountain;

from then on, the shrine no longer possessed spiritual efficacy. This is an example of how beings in the realm of ghosts undergo rebirth. Nowadays, ignorant commoners claim that [this is] the Buddha...
That Bodhisattvas are the same as ghosts and spirits—alas, how lamentable! △ Third, the refutation that those who receive the vital breath (*qi*) ought not to possess cognition, in two parts:
first, the formal refutation.
Furthermore, the vital breath of Heaven and Earth is fundamentally without cognition; since humans receive this insentient breath, how could they suddenly arise [with consciousness]?
There are those who know [this].
They ask: since *qi* (vital energy) is devoid of discrimination, how could a human being acquire it and yet possess discrimination?
If humans were to possess discrimination because they receive *qi*, then plants and trees should likewise possess discrimination, for that which they receive is the same. Thus it is argued.
One should also say: fundamentally, the qi of heaven and earth contains no distinction between the wise and the foolish, or the noble and the base;
how could it be that when humans receive this same [qi], they come to possess such distinctions of wisdom, folly, nobility, and baseness?

Yet Confucianists all insist on the theory of "receiving qi," claiming that those who receive pure and harmonious qi become sages or worthies, while those who receive turbid qi become fools or [the base].

Who among the unworthy does not know that the qi of heaven and earth is fundamentally without distinction, and that it is only due to the differences in the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ourselves?
It is like the sound from a flute or pipe, which varies according to the aperture through which it issues;

thus there are differences of clarity and turbidity, or high and low pitch, yet how could the breath of the one blowing it ever be different? If one were to claim that the breath of the blower is indeed different, [it would be a fallacy].

In that case, what need is there for the distinct apertures of bamboo pipes? Furthermore, as for the white peaches, red blossoms, yellow Yao-peonies, and purple Wei-peonies—is it not simply that the spring breeze varies for each?
Why do you not discern their inherent natures before blaming them on the external air?
△ This concludes the refutation by citing examples.
If grasses and trees also receive the vital breath (*qi*), why are they not conscious?
One might likewise ask: "Birds and beasts also all receive the vital breath; why then are their modes of flight and running so different?

It is because the *qi* of Heaven and Earth is like that of a furnace, a forge, or a steamer on a stove—it can only bring things into being but is not the inherent nature of the things themselves. Thus, the furnace and the forge...
Although one can cast metal into molds, one cannot transform copper or iron into fine gold; although a steamer may cook food, it cannot turn chaff and husks into delicacies.
Although the vital energy of Heaven and Earth can bring all things to completion, it cannot cause plants and trees to become human beings, nor can the vulgar and ignorant become sages.
This is because plants and trees each have their own roots, and humans and animals each have their own fundamental nature.
Therefore it is so. △ Fourth, the refutation of the doctrine of fate (fate-determinism), in two parts: First, restating their established position.
Furthermore, they say that poverty and wealth, nobility and meanness, worthiness and folly, good and evil, fortune and misfortune, and calamity and blessing all arise from the mandate of Heaven.
Many Confucian scholars hold this view; the former masters explained it by saying that "ming" (fate) is synonymous with "ling" (command).

Their school maintains that when pure qi ascends to the highest, unsurpassed point, it is called "Heaven. In this passage, the meaning is first restated. △ Next follows the formal refutation in three parts:
first, the refutation regarding the inequality in the distribution of calamities and blessings; first, the presentation of the refutation.

If Heaven’s allotment of destiny is indeed so, how can there be such abundance of the poor and scarcity of the wealthy, an abundance of the lowly and scarcity of the noble, and even an abundance of calamities and scarcity of blessings?
Since the Way of Heaven is said to be supremely impartial and equitable— without bias or partiality— why is it that there exist poverty, wealth, nobility, and meanness?

Furthermore, regarding the differences in the abundance or scarcity of merit and misfortune among the wise and the foolish, it is observed within this world that those who are poor, lowly, afflicted by calamity, or meet an early death are many, while those who are wealthy, noble, long-lived, and healthy are few.
Is this not evident to the eyes of all in the ways of the world? Why is this so? △ This concludes the section on the refutation of objections.
If the distinction between much and little resides in Heaven, why is Heaven not impartial?
If Heaven were truly such as this, where would its fairness and justice lie? △ Second, the irrationality of the inversion of calamity and fortune is difficult to reconcile;
Part One: A direct refutation.

How much more so when there is non-action esteemed and action disparaged; the possession of virtue rendered poor and the lack of virtue made wealthy; the auspicious deemed perverse and the inauspicious treated as righteous;
the benevolent met with early death and the violent granted long life; even to the point that those who possess the Way perish while those who lack the Way flourish.
There are those who act without restraint yet are esteemed like Jie and Zhou as rulers; there are those who maintain their conduct yet are held in low regard like Zhongni.
There are those with neither rank nor virtue yet possess wealth like Lord Jing, who owned a thousand teams of horses, or He Zeng, who daily consumed ten thousand coins.

Conversely, there are those with virtue yet live in poverty like Yuan Xian and Qianlou. Thus, there are instances where the perverse bring good fortune while the righteous meet with misfortune, such as when the wicked and treacherous attain power while the loyal suffer.

There are those like Liang who were harmed by others, and those like Ren who died young while the violent lived long lives; there are those like Yan Hui and Ran Geng who met with premature death, and those like Zibo who lived out their full spans.
Regarding the presence or absence of the Way, we see that virtuous people of the world often encounter misfortune at every turn, while the strong, arrogant, and greedy prosper in every undertaking.
From antiquity to the present, such cases have occurred repeatedly, leading worldly people to constantly claim that Heaven is unjust, or to say: [and so forth].

The Buddha, for the sake of beginners, initially taught the retribution of karma across the three periods of time—the causes and effects of good and evil.
"Beginners" refers to the specific capacity of those to be converted; they are called "beginners" in contrast to the subsequent three vehicles, as they are directed toward a single path.

Therefore, it is said that we shall first discuss the karmic retribution of the three periods of time: this refers to karma created in the past being experienced as retribution in the present life, and karma created in the present life being experienced as retribution in a future life. Hence, "karma of the three periods" refers to the causes that bring about results, while "retribution" refers to the results brought about by those causes.
Since both karma and retribution encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, they are called the "causes and effects of good and evil."
As explained in detail below. △ Second, the specific enumeration of the two [types of causes and effects]. First, the enumeration of the causes and effects of evil:
namely, committing the ten unwholesome actions of the superior grade leads to rebirth in hell; the middle grade, to the realm of hungry ghosts; and the inferior grade, to the realm of animals.

The ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) refer to the three of the body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the four of speech—false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech;

and the three of the mind—covetousness, malice, and wrong view. Regarding what is called "superior" (*adhimātra*): generally speaking, both wholesome and unwholesome deeds are categorized into three grades.
To clarify this by way of the object (*viṣaya*), for instance, killing a human being constitutes the superior grade, while killing an animal constitutes the middling grade.

1. Regarding the object: To refrain from killing humans is superior, while to refrain from killing mosquitoes and gnats is inferior; conversely, to refrain from killing humans is superior, whereas to refrain from killing mosquitoes and gnats is inferior.

2. Regarding the mind: Without considering whether the act is virtuous or non-virtuous, an intense and focused mind constitutes the superior grade, a casual and indifferent mind constitutes the inferior grade, and a mediocre, lukewarm mind constitutes the intermediate grade.
3. Regarding the time: Whether the act is virtuous or non-virtuous, if there is no regret during the three periods [of preparation, execution, and completion], it is considered superior.
The first two periods are "without regret," the middle period is "with regret," and the final period is "inferior. Regarding the mention of "hell" (*naraka*) and so forth:
in Sanskrit it is called *naraka*, which here means "vessel of suffering"—that is, the vessel in which sentient beings undergo suffering.

The current term "hell" (*diyu*) is established as a name based on its meaning: "earth" (*di*) refers to the bottom, and "prison" (*yu*) refers to confinement; because there are prisons beneath the earth, it is named thus.
There are four general categories of hells, namely: the eight hot hells, the eight cold hells, the neighboring hells (*utsada*), and the solitary hells (*pratyeka*).
Regarding the eight hot hells: the first is called Saṃjīva (Reviving). This refers to when one is hacked and chopped into thousands of pieces by swords and blades;

these fragments are then gathered together with forks and one cries out, "Live! Live! Thereupon, one immediately revives. Having revived, one is hacked again; having been hacked, one revives once more. For this reason, it is called Saṃjīva.
Five hundred years in the life-span of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings constitutes one day and night; by such accumulation, reaching five hundred years [is their full lifespan].
Second is the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell, where four mountains close together and crush the bodies of those with transgressions until they are like fine dust.
One thousand years in the life-span of the Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three) constitutes one day and night; by accumulating such months and years, their lifespan reaches one thousand years.

The third is Kālasūtra (Black Rope), where, as in the world, wood is split by saws guided by black ropes; their lifespan is two thousand years, with the two-thousand-year lifespan of the Yāma Heaven serving as one day and night.
The fourth is Raurava (Crying Out), where the four-thousand-year lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven serves as one day and night, and their lifespan is four thousand years.
The fifth is Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out), [where the lifespan is calculated] by that of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Eight thousand years constitutes one day and night; their lifespan is eight thousand years. Sixth is the Heat (Tapana) hell:
sixteen thousand years of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods constitutes one day and night; their lifespan is sixteen thousand years. Seventh is the Intense Heat (Pratāpana) hell:
its lifespan is half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), meaning that from the human lifespan of eighty-four thousand years, it decreases by one hundred years each year.
Decreasing by one year down to ten years is called a half intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); this constitutes the lifespan of this hell. Eighth is Avīci, which means "Without Interval" (*anantara*).
It is established with the name "Without Interval" for five reasons: first, the absence of interval in the performance of karma, explained in terms of punishment;
second, the absence of interval in the receiving of retribution, explained in terms of the fruit of maturation; third, the absence of interval in the experiencing of suffering.
Regarding the four [types of suffering] explained in terms of agony: fifth, there is no interval in the size of the body;
that is to say, due to their own respective karma, sentient beings each perceive their own bodies filling the interior of the hell such that there is no empty space between them;
therefore it is called "Avīci" (No-Interval). The lifespan in this hell is one *kalpa* of increase and decrease. As for the eight cold hells, they are properly called *Aṭaṭa*.

1. Arbuda (translated as "blister"): because the body, touched by the cold suffering, becomes like a blister or ulcer. 2. Nirarbuda ("bursting blisters"): because the frozen body cracks and splits open.

(These two names are established based on the characteristic of suffering. 3. Aṭaṭa ("shivering"), 4. Hahava ("wailing"), 5. Huhuva ("groaning")—these three names are established based on the sounds produced while experiencing suffering.
6. Utpala ("Blue Lotus"), 7. Padma ("Red Lotus"), 8. Mahāpadma ("Great Red Lotus")—the bodies, touched by the suffering of the cold, transform into these [lotus-like shapes].
Regarding the lifespan in these eight cold hells, there are two differing explanations. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is even longer than the preceding [hot hells].
However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the lifespans in the eight cold hells decrease by half in successive order compared to those in the eight hot hells;
for example, Arbuda is half the length of Saṃjīva, and this continues until Mahāpadma, which is likewise half the length of Avīci.

Based on this, the eight cold hells are lighter than the eight hot hells. Regarding the three neighboring hells (*utsada-naraka*), there are four such hells at each of the four gates of the eight hot hells:

The first is called *Kukūla* (Boiling Ashes), where the ashes reach up to the knees; when one lowers the feet, they are scorched and rotted away, yet when the feet are raised, they are restored as before.

The second is called *Kuṇapa* (Corpse Excrement), where the excrement and mud reach up to the knees; within it dwell venomous insects that devour the flesh as soon as one lowers the feet. When the feet are raised, [the flesh is restored].
The third [hell] is called "Razor Blades," where roads are covered with the edges of razors, swords, and other blades; when one treads upon them, they cut and wound.
The fourth is the "River of Ashes," a boiling, scalding lye where one is either boiled or stewed until the skin and flesh are decomposed and putrefied.
The four "Hells of Solitude" have no fixed location; they exist in places such as mountain ranges, beneath trees, in wildernesses, or at city walls and moats, depending on their conditions.
The *Ga-sūtra* states that those in the neighboring realms are solitary and their lifespans are indefinite, varying according to the length of their karma.
As for those called *preta* (hungry ghosts), they are so named because they endure hunger for long periods. Their degrees of suffering vary, and there are generally nine categories.
Twenty days in the human realm constitute one day and night for them; thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months [constitute a year].

Regarding the statement that "though the rituals differ"—such as in the case of the calendar, clothing, and caps—these vary according to region;

yet regarding the statement that "in admonishing evil and encouraging good there is no difference," this means they are largely identical to this land (China). Regarding the statement that "they also do not depart from benevolence and so forth," although virtuous conduct is manifold, citing its major outlines, it does not exceed these five [wholesome paths];

this can be seen therein. Thus, the ultimate principle of the world returns to one, and the minds of the sages fit together like two halves of a tally. It is not that Zhou and Confucius specially created these models for the sake of the people alone, nor is it that the Tathāgata merely imitated this land to establish his teachings. For example, the following provides an illustration by comparing the rites of Tibet with those of China.

The differences used as analogies between India and China are likewise so; I have briefly cited one aspect of ritual to illustrate the fourfold nature of benevolence and righteousness. Thus we know that the rituals and music of various nations differ from one another; one should discuss their underlying intentions rather than demanding conformity in their outward practices.
Otherwise, if those who adhere to a single local custom were to mock and marvel at one another, how could this be considered a comprehensive discourse?
If one who upholds the five precepts reverses the ten non-virtuous actions mentioned above, these are collectively termed the ten virtuous actions (*daśa-kuśala*).

Thus, it is stated in the second stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* that the ten virtuous actions serve as the cause for all five vehicles: namely, the lower grade serves as the cause for humans, the middle grade for devas, the upper grade for the three vehicles, and the highest of the upper grades for Buddhahood.
Furthermore, within the system of ethical discipline (*vinaya*), the Buddha additionally prescribed the five precepts for lay followers (*upāsaka*).
Since the precepts also apply to all five vehicles, one knows that the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths are largely the same with minor differences;

their expansion or contraction is according to what is appropriate, much like the six perfections and ten perfections of the Mahāyāna. (Note: Regarding "Non-killing is benevolence," the commentators below correlate the five precepts with the Five Constant Virtues because they share the same underlying meaning.

Thus, Master Mingjiao said: First is non-killing, which means one ought to love living beings and must not recklessly harm even a single thing, let alone eat its flesh. Mencius said, "To kill one innocent person is not benevolence. Therefore, [non-killing] is...)

1. "Not killing" as an act of benevolence means that one who does not steal is said to be righteous; it refers to not taking what is not given and ceasing from seizing the property of others. As Mencius said: "To take what is not one's own is unrighteous. 2.

"Not committing sexual misconduct" means not to become disordered with those who are not one's proper match. Because the rites distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, being consistent with this is called not committing sexual misconduct. 3. "Not engaging in false speech" means not deceiving others with one's words. Because the faithful do not alter their words, this is equivalent to not engaging in falsehood. 4.

"Not drinking or eating [intoxicants]" is because through drinking and eating, the mind and spirit become turbid and disordered, and the emotions and thoughts become deluded and frantic, thereby harming wisdom. Therefore, by not drinking or eating, the intellect and thought remain pure and clear. However, while other explanations merely say "not drinking," Guifeng added "not eating meat," which must have a specific basis.

According to some methods, it is encouraged that people adopt these as a gradual means for ceasing killing. These five precepts are entirely based on the teachings of the Buddha; however, within the *vinaya* (discipline), there are further distinctions regarding whether they are "complete" (*sakala*) or "incomplete" (*vikala*).

If one can maintain all five, it is called "complete" (*sakala*). If one can maintain only four, three, two, or fewer, it is called "incomplete" (*vikala*). If one maintains them for the duration of one's life, it is called "complete in duration" (*sakala-kāla*). If one can maintain them for only ten years, five years, or down to a single day, it is called "incomplete in duration" (*vikala-kāla*).

When these factors of "precept" (*aṅga*) and "duration" (*kāla*) are compared, there should be four possible permutations of completeness and incompleteness. Based on this, there are the categories of *upāsaka*, *upāsikā*, and *brahmacārin*. *Upāsaka* is translated as "male lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*); *upāsikā* is the female term. *Note: The original text contains the term *upāsaka* (優婆塞) and *upāsikā* (優婆夷). In the translation, these have been rendered phonetically with their respective English meanings provided.*

Furthermore, among these five precepts: because of the omission of non-killing, even if one obtains a human body, one suffers from many illnesses and a short lifespan; because of the omission of non-stealing, one lacks sufficient wealth and resources; because of the omission of non-sexual misconduct, one has no excellent retinue; because of the omission of non-lying, no one accepts what one says;

and because of the omission of non-drinking, the various faculties are dull and obscured. Moreover, among these five, the first four are *prakṛti-saṃvara* (natural precepts), meaning that killing, stealing, and so forth are offenses by their very nature; thus they are called natural precepts. The single precept regarding drinking alcohol is a *prajñapti-saṃvara* (prohibitory precept);

it is so called because drinking alcohol disturbs the nature and leads to the violation of the previous four precepts. Therefore, the Buddha established this [precept] to prevent those four, and thus it is termed a prohibitory precept.
To say that one "attains exemption from the three miserable realms" refers to being free from evil; to say that one "is born into the human realm" refers to the fruit thus elicited.
Now, the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths are all received from a teacher. It is said that this body of the precepts is obtained the moment the words of the Three Refuges are uttered;

or, if one first receives the Three Refuges and subsequently receives the five or ten precepts—there has never been anyone who attained the precepts without taking refuge in the Triple Gem. This is because...

Because one takes refuge in the Buddha, one does not fall into hell; because one takes refuge in the Dharma, one does not fall among the hungry ghosts; because one takes refuge in the Sangha, one does not fall among the animals.

What is now said regarding the avoidance of the three miserable realms is due to the power of the Three Refuges. Since the reception of the five precepts must necessarily be preceded by the Three Refuges, they are not mentioned here in brief.

Regarding the practice of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) of the superior grade, there are two intended meanings: First, in contrast to the preceding five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), these are termed "superior," for the five precepts are considered inferior;
thus, what is here called "superior" refers specifically to the ten wholesome actions. Second, this is an elliptical expression used for clarity.

It implies that among humans, the ten wholesome actions are considered inferior (as they were not explicitly mentioned previously because they were already contained within the five precepts), whereas among the devas, they are considered superior. Thus, the ten wholesome actions of the superior grade are distinguished [from those of the human realm].

Because they are of inferior grade, furthermore, among the gods, the ten wholesome paths (*daśa-kuśala*) serve as the general category, while giving and the other perfections act as the specific instances.

This means that practicing the ten wholesome paths together with a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), while concurrently performing acts such as giving, leads to birth in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). When practiced together with a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), one is born in the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the "ten wholesome paths," killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are identical to the first five precepts (*pañca-śīla*). The fifth—refraining from frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*)—means not...

Sixth, not glossing over one's faults; seventh, not using double-tongued speech, meaning one does not speak differently behind someone's back; eighth, not using harsh speech, meaning one’s words are always kind and compliant;
ninth, not being covetous, meaning the mind is constantly content and does not give rise to defiled attachment toward existence or the requisites for existence;
tenth, not being angry, meaning one does not harbor resentment in the heart; eleventh, not holding wrong views, meaning the mind and vision are correct.
These six precepts—uprightness, absence of deceit, and absence of flattery—are enumerated with slight variations in different teachings, yet they do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, in one sutra, the four aspects of speech are condensed into three: non-slander, non-deceit, and non-falsehood;

these, together with the addition of "not drinking alcohol and not eating meat," constitute four. In the *Avataṃsaka*, among the four types of speech, false speech is [treated as the primary concern].
Divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech follow next; this sequence is established according to their relative gravity.

Master Song’s *Fǔjiào biān* lists the three mental afflictions (*māna*, *vyāpāda*, and *mithyādṛṣṭi*) as envy, anger, and delusion (therefore, the previous explanation of greed was distinct, relying instead on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*). The *Yíngluò jīng* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* restrict these [afflictions] solely to the Mahāyāna, so they are not included here.
Nevertheless, regarding how these three mental afflictions can constitute paths of action (*karmapatha*), the *Qīngliáng Dàshù* states:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, if greed is not yet determined, it is merely termed an affliction (*kleśa*); once it is determined, it is termed karma (*karman*). The same applies to hatred and delusion.
Among the three types of intentional action, one must fulfill five conditions for it to constitute a course of karmic action (*karmapatha*).

These five conditions are: first, the object (generally referring to another's property, as it is possessed by another); second, the substance (the specific substance of what is craved, such as gold, silver, wealth, or treasures); third, the distinction; within this [third condition], there are three [subdivisions].

1. Not seeking (seeking begins with the desire for another's object); 2. Not wishing (desiring to acquire it for oneself is aspiration); 3. Not coveting (ultimately giving rise to the thought of seizing it constitutes greed).

Within these distinctions, the first two are the preliminary applications (*prayoga*), the last one is the consummation (*niṣṭhā*), and together with the preceding objective basis (*vastu*), there are five conditions.
Among these five, if the consummation is missing, it is merely termed an affliction; when good and evil are opposed, they constitute [the respective paths].
The principle of karma is likewise.

Regarding the mention of generosity and ethical discipline: when one observes the ten wholesome paths of action and extensively practices giving, one experiences the retribution of the desire-realm heavens, where food and clothing appear spontaneously, palaces follow one’s person, and one is surrounded by a retinue of attendants; such fruits and rewards arise from generosity.
Therefore, the long lifespans of devas and humans are due to the observance of precepts (*śīla*).

Although "ten wholesome actions" were mentioned previously, the present mention of "precepts" likely refers to either the *upavāsa* (one-day) precepts or the monastic precepts (*pravrajyā-śīla*), as explained in the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness), which states that there are those who observe the *upavāsa* precepts for one day and one night, or the *śrāmaṇera* (novice) and *bhikṣu* (fully ordained) precepts; thus they are distinguished here.

The phrase "and so forth" includes patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or other wholesome dharmas—such as making offerings to the Triple Gem, being filial toward one's parents, and cultivating the eight fields of merit.
However, the ten wholesome paths of action alone constitute the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*); all others are auxiliary causes.
Because these are cultivated with a mind that is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), they do not exempt one from saṃsāra, unlike the bodhisattvas who have access to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the statement "born in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth," the term "heavens" is used generally. The *Abhidharmakośa* states that they are designated as such because they possess radiant purity, mastery, and divine efficacy;
collectively they comprise the three realms, and specifically twenty-eight heavens. These are:

the six heavens of the desire realm, the eighteen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As for the "desire realm," it refers to food, drink, and sleep.

Because there is mutual affection between men and women, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding the six heavens: the first is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), whose lifespan is five hundred years;
one day and night there is equivalent to fifty human years, and their cycle of yin and yang is like that of the human world.
The second is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (translated as "The Thirty-three"), whose lifespan is one thousand years; one day and night there is equivalent to one hundred human years.

At night, they embrace one another as their union of yin and yang. In the third heaven, Yāma (translated as "Time" or "Divisions"), day and night are determined by the opening and closing of lotus flowers;
thus it is called "Time. Their lifespan is two thousand years, where two hundred human years constitute a single day and night.
They engage in the union of yin and yang by drawing their bodies close together. In the fourth heaven, Tuṣita (translated as "Contentment"),...
Because they are always content with the pleasures they receive, their lifespan is twice that of the former [Heaven of Joy], being four thousand years.

Four hundred human years constitute one day and night there; they engage in sexual union by holding hands. In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), beings create their own objects of pleasure according to their own minds and enjoy them themselves;
therefore, their lifespan is eight thousand years. Eight [human years... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here].
One hundred years constitutes a single day and night; by such reckoning, six [such days] form a cycle of yin and yang.

The sixth heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations), is so called because its inhabitants enjoy the objects emanated by others as their own. Their lifespan is sixteen thousand years.
One thousand six hundred human years constitute a single day and night for them; by such reckoning, a mere blink of an eye forms a cycle of yin and yang. From this point onward...
It is still called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the statement "cultivating the four dhyānas and eight samādhis," the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*zhènglǜ*). The *Fayuan zhang* states:

"Calm" (*jìng*) refers to being detached from the clamor and dust of the world, as well as from hindrances such as mental sinking and agitation; "contemplation" (*lǜ*) refers to concentrating the mind on a single purpose and deliberating upon the object.

To explain: among the various formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there is tranquility (*śānti*) but no investigation (*vitarka*); because they consist solely of a concentrated mind, they lack the investigative function.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and its associated states, there is investigation but no tranquility; because they are largely characterized by distraction and movement, they lack stability. Only within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and tranquility balanced;

therefore, it receives this designation. Regarding the four dhyānas: the first is "meditative absorption with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Applied thought and sustained thought are also termed "initial inquiry (*vitarka*)" and "subsequent examination (*vicāra*"); these are the antidotes [to the distractions of the lower realms].
Because of the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm, there is vitarka (applied thought) based on coarse characteristics and vicāra (sustained thought) based on subtle characteristics.

Second, the dhyāna without vitarka and without vicāra arises because one leaves behind the mind of initial and sustained application (*vitarka-vicāra*) from the preceding first dhyāna and gives rise to joy (*prīti*).

Third, the dhyāna free from joy leaves behind the joyful mind of the preceding second dhyāna; as both sorrow and joy are forgotten, one dwells in the feeling of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*). Fourth, [the dhyāna] free from...
Regarding the "joy and bliss of dhyāna," because joy, bliss, suffering, and pleasure are all forgotten beyond the first three dhyānas, they are called the eight concentrations (*aṣṭa-samādhi*).
Following the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are added: First is the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*):

one completely transcends all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) previously present within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Second is the [attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness]... form.
In the preparatory stage for the Sphere of Infinite Space, both form and space were not separate from consciousness; now, having transcended both, one dwells solely in infinite consciousness.
In the preparatory stage for the Sphere of Nothingness, there was still consciousness in which to dwell;
now, even consciousness cannot be apprehended, because both mind and its objects are non-existent. [In the preparatory stage] for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception...
Because one is now able to be free from the conceptualizations of mind and consciousness, this [state] is likewise called "concentration" (*samādhi*) together with the four dhyānas;
for within the four dhyānas there exists a portion of definitive concentration, and thus they receive the designation of "concentration.

As for those who are born into the form and formless realms by virtue of practicing the four dhyānas: it is called the "form realm" (*rūpa-dhātu*) because they possess a physical body composed of the five aggregates.
"Formless" (*ārūpya*) means that there is no coarse aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), but only the four aggregates;

because the mind and mental factors abide supported by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). (Note: Regarding the lower part of the title, this anticipates a potential objection: "Since this [text] clearly explains all five destinies (*gati*), why does the title only designate 'the original person' (*yuanren*) and not mention the heavens and so forth?

First, the note restates the objection regarding the differences between realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*); second, it provides the formal response: one should say that the realms and destinies differ, or perhaps it is a scribal error. The three miserable paths, humans, and devas each have distinct classes of destiny (*gati*), and the desire, form, and formless realms differ according to their supporting stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, it is said "seen and heard.")

As for those who do not reach [this level], it is said that the realms of heaven, hell, and the hungry ghosts were not discussed by Confucius and Laozi, nor are they seen by the eyes of the mundane; thus it is so stated. Regarding those of the common world and below, speaking in terms of the capacities of those to be taught: even those who do not know the "branches" (the secondary) take heaven as the "root" and humans and animals as the "branches.

Worldly people only know that humans, animals, plants, and trees are produced based on heaven; they do not know that humans and animals are summoned by their own karma, yet they falsely claim they are born from heaven. This is ignorance of the branches, let alone knowing what the fruits of those heavens and so forth actually are.

Even if one were to speak of them, one would merely say that pure qi ascends to be lofty, bright, and enduring—without sound or smell—regarding this as the ultimate. Furthermore, they do not believe in the Buddha’s teachings which can exhaustively describe the entirety of heaven and earth.

Since this is the reality, how could one possibly exhaustively investigate the root? How much less could one know that "emptiness arises from great awakening, like a single bubble on the ocean"? Therefore, these two phrases following [the previous section] serve to conclude the intended meaning; they originate from the intent of establishing the title. Now, the subsequent passage sets forth the intent of this specific text.

The phrase "Therefore it is called... concludes the section, which is easily understood. In the commentary, the passage beginning with "However, karma exists... distinguishes the differences between karmic retribution. "Karma" (業) takes "constructive activity" as its definition. However, in terms of essence, there are the provisional and the real: body and speech are provisional, while volition (*cetanā*) is the real entity. Furthermore, there are three types of volition:

namely, deliberation (*vitarka*), determination (*vicāra*), and the impulse to initiate action (*pravartaka*). Only when the impulse to initiate action is present does it constitute a *karmapatha* (path of action). Specifically, the volition that moves the body is the reality of bodily action, and the volition that initiates speech is the reality of vocal action. The two types of volition—deliberation and determination—are merely...

Regarding the presence or absence of these intentional mental actions (*manas-karman*), as explained in the *Fayuan zhang*: First, the "unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala-karmapatha*) of the preceding three categories. Second, the "wholesome" refers to the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*), and so forth. Third, "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*) refers to the four dhyānas and eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) mentioned previously;

because they are not moved by the agitation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are termed "immovable. As for the statement that "retribution also has three times," the meaning of retribution (*vipāka*) is defined as recompense for a cause. "Retribution in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) means that one receives the fruit of good or evil deeds performed in the present within that same lifetime.

This is like taking a potent medicine against wolves or tigers and seeing its effect immediately; it is because such karma is produced with an extremely intense and sharp mind that it attains retribution in the present life. An example is King Virūḍhaka (Liu-li-wang), who, having massacred the Śākya clan, was reborn and fell into the Avīci hell. Furthermore, Master Fazu attained realization through single-minded recollection.

Those born in the presence of Amitābha and reborn in the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) do not again pass through an intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Second, retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*) refers to actions performed in this life whose results are received in the following life, just as one sows wheat this year and harvests it the next. Third, retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*) refers to actions performed in this life whose results are received only after a further birth has passed.

This is like two people who have contracted debts; whichever creditor is more pressing first drags them away. If good karma is light and evil karma is heavy, one first receives the evil retribution; if evil karma is light and good karma is heavy, one first receives the good retribution. Thus, that which is received later is designated as "subsequent retribution.

This classification of priority based on the intermingling of good and evil, and further by their relative weight, is according to this [text]. Other sutras and treatises state that in addition to these three, there is also "indeterminate retribution" (*aniyata-vedanīya-karman*). When examining these in relation to the timing [of their fruition], there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, those that are simultaneous...

(1) karma with fixed retribution and indefinite timing; (2) karma with indefinite retribution and fixed timing; (3) karma with both retribution and timing fixed; (4) karma with both retribution and timing indefinite, and so forth). △ Third, the summary:
According to these teachings, karma is the fundamental basis of the body.
Regarding "karma is the root of the body": one merely knows that this body is summoned by karma, yet does not further investigate from where karma itself comes.

This is because their faculties are dull and they are unable to exhaustively investigate the matter. This is like the calculations of the masters of past-action theory (*pūrvakṛtavādin*) in the Western regions;
seeing that one performs good deeds in this life yet suffers in the present, or performs evil deeds yet experiences pleasure, they then form this [view].
If one considers that what is performed by a person in the present life must necessarily be inverted [in its result], one should know that it is due to their karmic actions in past lives;
therefore, performing good deeds in this life can destroy those past karmas, and once past karma is exhausted, one attains nirvāṇa and so forth.
△ Third, the refutation of that [position] through interrogation, in two parts: first, a general interrogation regarding the agent and the experiencer.
Now, I interrogate him, saying: "Since one undergoes the bodies of the five destinies due to the creation of karma, it is not yet clear who creates the karma and who receives the retribution.
He should answer: "It is none other than my own body and mind that are capable of creating [it]. △ Next, I follow his tracks to present a further objection.

Within this, there are two initial sections concerning the difficulty of the body and mind being distinct; within these, there are again two parts, the first of which addresses the difficulty regarding the body.
First, it restates their position:
"If it were the eyes, ears, hands, or feet that are capable of performing actions..."

One should further interrogate them, saying: "As for your claim that the body and mind can create [the world], the body that you say creates is nothing more than the eyes, ears, hands, feet, and so forth.
If this is the case... (and so on), which restates their established position. △ Next, the actual presentation of the refutation.
When a person has just died, their eyes, ears, hands, and feet remain intact; why then do they not see, hear, or act?
"Intact" means clearly present. This argument uses the present as an analogy for the past.

This objection arises because [the opponent] fails to understand that the body and so forth are provisional constructs, and instead clings to them as real entities capable of acting. △ Second, the refutation of the mind (citta) in two parts:
First, the general objection has two parts: first, establishing the premise; second, the formal objection.
If it is said that the mind creates [it], [then...
△ Second, the formal objection.

What is this "mind"? Because his previous arguments regarding the body were defeated by these challenges, he then shifted his position and clung to the mind; therefore, [the interlocutor] now interrogates him, saying: "As for this 'mind' you speak of, what exactly is it?
Now, according to the Buddhist teachings, there are generally four kinds of mind: first, the lump-of-flesh mind (*piṇḍa-citta*). Fifth... [text fragment].
1. The "fire-treasury" mind; 2. The "contemplative" mind, which refers to the eight consciousnesses as they all can contemplate their respective objects;
3. The "accumulating-and-arising" mind, which refers exclusively to the *ālayavijñāna* because it accumulates all seeds and gives rise to manifest activities (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);
4. The "solid-core" mind, which is the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. People of the human and celestial realms do not understand these latter three, and thus they invite [suffering].
This objection is largely identical to the conventional [objection] regarding the mind. △ Second, the specific refutation of the two [positions]: first, the physical heart;
second, the formal refutation.
If one says that the physical heart has a material substance and is bound within the body, how could it enter the eyes and ears so swiftly to discern external objects?
Regarding this "is" and "is not," one does not know on what basis to accept or reject it.
As for those who claim there is a substantial entity, they assert that the "flesh-ball mind" (māṃsapiṇḍa-citta) belongs to the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*);

however, it is merely the support for the mind and its associates, lacking any real functional activity. As for how [the mind] can enter the eyes, ears, and so forth so rapidly: the Buddha taught that the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*)...

There are two functional aspects: first, that which operates simultaneously with the five consciousnesses; for example, when the eye perceives form, the mind (*manas*) also perceives form, discriminating between black and white and giving rise to specific conceptualizations.
The same applies to the ear perceiving sound and so forth. Second, that which does not operate with the five [consciousnesses] and is termed "solitary" (*mukhya*) mind;
this refers to instances such as internal reflection when the aforementioned five do not perceive external objects. This is what people nowadays [refer to].

The objection raised by the Celestial Teacher stems from his failure to recognize that it is the function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to perceive external objects, which he mistakenly identifies as the mind itself;
thus, this difficulty arises. △ Second, the conclusion of the objection:

Furthermore, since the mind and the eyes, ears, hands, and feet are all characterized by material resistance (*sapratigha*), how could they possibly communicate between the internal and external, such that movement would be possible?

This connects with the conditions for the simultaneous creation of karma, demonstrating that the physical heart-mass has no functional activity. If it were to possess such function, then the lungs and other organs should likewise do so;

consequently, those who have already died would be capable of cognitive apprehension. △ Second, the refutation of the attachment to the notion of mental apprehension, in two parts: first, restating their salvific argument.
If one were to say that it is only joy, anger, love, and hatred that incite the body and speech to create karma, one fears the opponent might argue:
"It is the mind (*citta*) that can experience joy, anger, love, and hatred and incite the body and speech; therefore, it is the mind that creates karma.

This would be to mistake the emotional states for the mind itself, without realizing that joy, anger, and so forth are merely mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). △

Later, when interrogated through reasoning, [it is seen that] emotions such as joy and anger arise and perish in an instant; since they lack an inherent substance of their own, what could serve as the master to perform actions?
That which arises and perishes in an instant means that toward objects of a favorable nature, one feels joy and attachment, while toward objects of an adverse nature, one feels... [anger].
If anger arises when an unpleasant object appears, and ceases when that object departs, you fail to realize that the essence of the mind is eternal and fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing.
