Since there are similarities and differences between what these two traditions teach, they must be harmonized and explained to resolve doubts. First, regarding the "harmonizing discussion" (*huì-yì*), this refers to the treatise.

The main critique states: "The phrase 'reaching the Way of Non-existence within the kalpa of emptiness' is the primary heading and also restates the doubt raised by the opponent. This is because one might suspect that the Buddhist "kalpa of emptiness" (śūnya-kalpa) is not actually the "Way of Non-existence" (wú-xū zhī dào) spoken of by Laozi, given that the term "non-existence" (wú-xū) shares the same meaning as "emptiness" (śūnyatā).

Furthermore, since it is said to have arisen before heaven and earth, its timing appears to coincide with that [of the Daoist view]. The intent of this treatise is to say that they appear similar when described in broad terms; hence it is stated thus. However, the section beginning with "the essence of the Dao" clarifies that, upon ultimate investigation, they differ:

Buddhism speaks of the "kalpa of emptiness" in contrast to the periods of formation, abiding, and destruction, referring exclusively to a state of voidness, rather than the "emptiness" of the True Emptiness and Wondrous Existence (zhēn kōng miào yǒu). As for the substance of the Dao, it is supremely wondrous, pervasive, and non-affiliated with either emptiness or existence. If one were to take [Buddhist] emptiness as...

The Way [described by] Laozi is not the True Way. [This section] provides a comprehensive explanation of his methods of negation and affirmation. First, negation is employed to manifest their differences. While it is not certain that Laozi’s intent was definitively to point to the "empty kalpa" (*śūnyakalpa*) as "non-existence" (*vibhava*), his statements such as "that which arose before heaven and earth" and "the Dao gave birth to...

appear to correspond to that period. Fearing that later generations might fail to understand this and instead point to the empty kalpa itself, thereby falling into dogmatic attachment, he says, "they are deluded. However, the empty kalpa refers to time, whereas non-existence refers to the essence of the Way; how could these be the same? Alternatively, through the provisional application of negation and affirmation, they are shown to be identical. In reality, the Way is neither empty nor existent;

it does not hinder being within emptiness while being identical to emptiness, nor does it hinder being within existence while being identical to existence. Now, because Laozi bases himself on the Way existing prior to heaven and earth, he calls it "non-existence. Furthermore, he seeks to remedy the defects of human beings.

Because worldly people cling to existence, Laozi says that the Great Dao is empty and non-existent; how could it ever have existence? Thus he says: "One must strive to sever human desires. Human desires are precisely the view of clinging to existence, as the *Daodejing* states: "The five colors blind the eyes; the five flavors dull the palate," and so forth.

Furthermore, the first chapter says: "Always being without desire, one observes its subtlety; always having desire, one observes its periphery. Is this not precisely what is meant by striving to sever human desires?

The great wind within the realm of emptiness is "the single qi"; this wind is the aforementioned wind that sustains the realm, which is the wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Chaos is when yin and yang have not yet differentiated; Laozi calls this the "qi of the profound" (*chong qi*). Therefore, the text below cites that passage to provide scriptural proof for the Way.

Because it moves and gives rise to the Qi of profound harmony (*chōng-hé*), it is said that "the Dao gives birth to the One. When the metal treasury is beneath the clouds, it accords with the Confucian doctrine of the five phases (*wùnyùn*). As for rain falling without flowing, this refers to the previous statement: "The rain was like the axle of a chariot, held back by the wind so that it could not flow.

If one takes this to be Yin Qi, then the metal treasury and the clouds must be taken as Yang Qi. Thus, while the single Qi previously mentioned transforms here into Yin and Yang, because they have not yet separated, it is said they are "in union," still belonging to the One.

Regarding the separate correlation of the Brahma King’s realm (*bànwángjiè*) with the Three Powers (*sāncái*), one may understand it by consulting the preceding treatise. That the treatise treats Heaven and Earth as two and the Three Powers as three is likely because the Master of the Treatise possessed a profound realization that accorded with Emperor Ming’s interpretation.

Differences can be understood through the underlying intent and need not necessarily adhere strictly to the literal text. Regarding the "earth-cake" (*dibing*) and so forth, its meaning is easy to comprehend. For one who understands the core of Confucianism, the period from Brahmā downward corresponds to the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) giving rise to the Two Polarities;

the period from the earth-cake downward corresponds to the Four Images (*sìxiàng*) giving rise to the Eight Trigrams (*bāguā*), and so on. As for the phrase "prior to the Three Sovereigns," according to secular classics, there are two traditions regarding the Three Sovereigns. The *Xugong Jini* (Annals of Duke Xu) and the *Jishi* (Compendium of Events), citing ancient and modern accounts, state: "At the beginning of primordial chaos, the pure qi ascended and the turbid qi descended.

At this time, Pangu appeared and governed for eighteen thousand years. After Pangu died, his form divided into material phenomena; thus there were mountains, rivers, plants, trees, sun, moon, clouds, and thunder. From this point on, there was the Heavenly Sovereign (*Tianhuangshi*) and the Earthly Sovereign (*Dihuangshi*)."

The Huang clan and the Renhuang clan—these were the names of the first three sovereigns, each governing for eighteen thousand years. Following them were the clans of Youchao and Suiren; it was only thereafter that Fuxi, Shennong, and the Yellow Emperor emerged as the latter three sovereigns.

Fuxi drew the eight trigrams and created writing and seals; Shennong fashioned the plow and hoe to sow the hundred grains and tasted medicinal herbs to cure various ailments. The Yellow Emperor established palaces, residences, clothing, boats, carts, and utensils, and standardized the rites of marriage and mourning.

In ancient times, people ate raw fur and drank blood, dwelling in caves and living in the wild, with no distinction between humans and animals. Since the emergence of Youchao, he taught the people to dwell in tree nests during the summer and in earthen caves during the winter, thereby changing their former practice of cave-dwelling and wilderness living.

When Fēngsuìrén (the Lord of the Wind and Fire Drill) arose and produced fire by drilling wood, people first began to cook their food; hence it is said that from before the Three Sovereigns until the advent of fire-refinement and so forth, matters are merely treated according to their respective eras. Anticipating potential doubts, one might ask:

"Since what is taught by Confucius and Laozi is identical to that of Buddhism, why does this land [China] not speak of the four wheels (*catur-cakra*) or the descent of the Ābhāsvara devas, but instead speaks of Pángǔ and others? Therefore, the *Lùn* (Treatise) explains: "In ancient times in this land, as there were no written records to be examined, we cannot obtain full details.

We now merely rely on the words of Lǎozǐ such as 'the Dao gives birth to all things' (*dào shēng yīqiè*) and the theory of the Five Phases (*wǔyùn*) of the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*), which possess principles roughly similar to those of Buddhism; thus, we harmonize them. This is further explained below in the Buddhist section.

The two teachings differ in their scope; thus, while this region has accounts reaching back to the very first emergence [of Buddhism], they generally know only that which lies within the four seas and nine provinces. However, what is described in earlier sūtras and śāstras such as the *Abhidharmakośa* refers universally to the realm ruled by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Regarding the "three thousandfold world system," the verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"One thousand sets of the four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the desire-realm heavens, and the Brahmā and Śakra heavens, is called a small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūdika-lokadhatu*). One thousand times this small thousandfold world system is called a medium thousandfold world system (*dvisāhasramadhyama-lokadhatu*).

One thousand times this [medium] is a great thousandfold world system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhatu*), all of which undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. When it is said that this does not limit [the teaching] to the Great Tang, the author of the treatise merely speaks according to the circumstances of his own time; that is to say, he refers to the land of Zhendan (China), as is the case in sūtras and śāstras such as the *Ratnarāśi* (Renwang jing).

It is said that in this Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great nations, two thousand middle nations, and one hundred thousand small nations; yet Zhendan (China) is not included within the number of the sixteen. Thus we know that in the previous assembly, Confucius and Laozi were merely intended to engage the capacities of those in this region.

In reality, the internal [Buddhist] and external [non-Buddhist] teachings cannot be entirely identical. Nevertheless, Zhuangzi says, "Beyond the Infinite there is again the Infinite," and he also says, "Beyond the six directions, the Sage exists but does not discuss them. This is because the timing and conditions had not yet reached them; thus Confucius and Laozi existed but did not speak of it.

However, the transformation of the Great Hero (the Buddha) universally covers the three-thousandfold world system and encompasses all five natures. That his net of teaching must be so vast and expansive was inevitable. Yet even these three thousand worlds are still limited when compared to the Small Vehicle teachings, let alone the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

It is merely like a hair-tip compared to the great void. Regarding the phrase "the abiding [kalpa]," the remaining three types of kalpas—abiding, forming, and destroying—can be understood through brief analysis. Within the context of the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (the kalpa of destruction), the statement that "the first nineteen [cycles] destroy sentient beings through increase and decrease" refers to the following:

at the end of one *apacaya-kalpa* (decreasing cycle), when the human lifespan is thirty years, the *durbhikṣa-kalpa* (famine kalpa) arises. For seven years, seven months, and seven days, a pervasive wind blows, causing the seasons to lose their regularity and the five grains to fail to grow; thus, famine ensues.

When the human lifespan is twenty years, the *roga-kalpa* (epidemic kalpa) arises, where malevolent spirits and ghosts inflict harm upon people, ceasing after seven months, seven days, and seven nights. When the human lifespan is ten years, the *śastra-kalpa* (sword-and-weapon kalpa) arises; all grasses and trees transform into swords and staves, and they slaughter one another. Only...

Adorned with swords and staves, they cease [their conflict] after seven days and seven nights; at that time, there should be no sentient beings remaining in the world—this is what is said according to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Regarding the subsequent increase and decrease that destroys the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*): first, when the calamity of fire arises, it destroys up to the First Dhyāna. When the seven suns arise in the sky, the great earth and Mount Sumeru all emit flames and simultaneously burn away.

Because of that heat, the water-wheel (*apmaṇḍala*) below is drawn upward like clarified butter until everything is exhausted. After seven such calamities of fire, there arises a calamity of water that destroys up to the Second Dhyāna. After seven calamities of water, there arises a calamity of wind that destroys up to the Third Dhyāna. Therefore, the treatise concludes: "That which is capable of destroying is fire and water."

The three calamities, such as wind and so forth, can be understood through the aeon of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kalpa*). Question: Since that time is empty, who then knows the number of its kalpas? Answer: It can be known by comparing it with the *kalpa* of abiding in other realms. Regarding the phrase "kalpa after kalpa," the lower part concludes that [the teaching] is inexhaustible; the first three lines explain this through the Dharma, while the final line clarifies it through a metaphor.

In the commentary, the forms are contrasted with worldly teachings to distinguish their relative superiority and inferiority; since the textual structure is easy to understand, the concluding statement below indicates that its merit transcends and surpasses others. As for the phrase "shallow and shallow teachings": when the latter four teachings are compared with the former ones, the former are shallow and the latter are deep;

this refers specifically to the shallowest among the shallow. If compared to the Human and Celestial (Śrāvaka) teachings, these are also relatively deep; however, they are not compared to those because the Human and Celestial teachings have not yet emerged from the triple world (*tridhātu*). The conclusion and demonstration has two parts:
first, clarifying the reason for saṃsāra, which arises entirely from failing to realize that this body is fundamentally not the self;
second, the explanation of non-self, which has two parts: first, the heading.
"It is not me. △ This is the formal explanation that follows:
it means that this body originally takes the form of a composite of matter and mind.
One should first ask: "Why does the cycle of birth and death continue without ceasing? The answer is: "It is entirely due to a failure to understand," and so forth;
thus, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, resulting in the cycle of birth and death. One asks: "Why is it not the self? The treatise states:

"That which is not the self" refers to the following explanation of *Perfect Enlightenment* (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), which says that sentient beings, from time immemorial, have falsely identified with the four [elements].
The great self is the characteristic of one's own body; the six sense-objects and their reflected shadows are the characteristics of one's own mind.
Sentient beings do not understand this and falsely reckon them as "self. Apart from form and mind, who is there that is the self? △ Second, the purification of the two [aspects], first:

Form (*rūpa*) consists of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; mind (*citta*) consists of feeling (*vedanā*, which is capable of experiencing pleasant and unpleasant matters), perception (*saṃjñā*, which is capable of grasping images), and formations (*saṃskāra*, which are capable of constructing...).
The fourth [mark] of consciousness is that its creator flows and shifts from moment to moment.
Regarding the statement "it is not the self" based on what preceded it: since it originally arises from the combination of form (rūpa) and mind (citta), the externalist asks:
"If the combination of form and mind is my very body, why do you say it is not the self? The answer is: this is due to the attachment of deluded sentiment.
When one clings [to phenomena], they seem to exist; yet when observed through analytical wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), one knows they are fundamentally non-existent.

This is because the ignorant *śrāvakas* do not realize that emptiness is manifest within form itself; they must rely on the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) to conceptually analyze phenomena before they can know them to be empty.
Thus, it is said: "investigating and analyzing. Regarding "form exists" and so forth: form has the characteristic of resistance and obstruction; however, form...

Form and appearance characterized by length, shortness, squareness, roundness, and so forth are called *saṃsthāna-rūpa* (shape-color); blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth are called *varṇa-rūpa* (manifest color).
Earth, water, fire, and wind are termed the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because these four dharmas pervade all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they are called "great.
As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "This body of mine now is a combination of the four great elements..."
That is to say: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these forms return to earth;
sexual fluids, tears, pus, blood, lymph, saliva, mucus, phlegm, sweat, semen, vital energy, feces, and urine—all these return to water;
warmth returns to fire; and movement returns to wind. When the four elements have thus been divided, where does form reside? As for the mind, it is likewise [without location].
The preceding aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is called "form" (*nāma*), while these four aggregates are called the "mental aggregate" (*citta-skandha*).

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of "accumulation," because many dharmas are accumulated to form a single aggregate. Feeling (*vedanā*) has the characteristic of experiencing; it is divided into three types: suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) has the characteristic of conceptualizing, such as apprehending a present object or recollecting past events. Formations (*saṃskāra*) have the characteristic of conditioning and flux.
Regarding their characteristics, there is a distinction between those associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*) and those not associated with the mind (*citta-viprayukta*).

First, as for those associated with the mind, among the forty-six mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of the Hīnayāna, all except for the two factors of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are included.

As for those not associated with the mind, there are fourteen kinds, as detailed in the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is defined by the meaning of "discernment" (*prativijñapti*); in the Hīnayāna, it is considered to be of only one kind.
Consciousness. △ Third, a concise summary of the three [aggregates].

the four are divided into sixteen parts, continuing until the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is reached, which is called the "dust-particle adjacent to emptiness" (*sūkṣma-rajas*). Only when it is indistinguishable from space is it termed "empty.

Regarding the skin and hair discussed below, these are cited according to their characteristics to make them easily understood; four examples are given for each of the internal and external [elements], each being distinct.
The characteristic is a single phrase that summarizes the many dharmas mentioned previously. Since these characteristics do not constitute a self, who then could be called the "I"?

as for the two great elements of fire and wind, although each is identical [in nature], they are described as different based on their respective faculties, such as in the cases of breathing, running, yawning, and so forth, where each function is distinct.
However, to explain the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) in general, there are eleven factors: namely, the five sense organs, the five objects, and non-informative form (*avijñaptirūpa*).

Since we are currently discussing only the body, the objects and so forth are not mentioned; these should be analyzed by analogy. [The second part,] the subsequent analysis of mind, has two sections. First, the heading.
The various mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth are likewise each distinct.
[This is] explained later.
Seeing is not hearing; joy is not anger; and so on, extending through the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because they are the various differentiated functional activities of the mind-king (*cittarāja*), they are called mental factors (*caitta*).
However, the mental factors of the Hīnayāna comprise forty-six dharmas, which are subsumed into six categories totaling fifty-one types of aspects;

these are detailed extensively as explained in other commentaries. Nevertheless, the intent of the present treatise is to demonstrate that there is no real self (*ātman*) herein; were one to attempt a minute analysis, it would be too extensive.

Regarding the statement about "losing the sheep": what is meant by "seeing, hearing, joy, and anger" is that seeing and hearing are easily understood, whereas joy and anger refer to what the Confucian tradition calls the "seven emotions.
These are not separate from the aforementioned dharmas of the mind; they are mentioned separately in various treatises simply to make them easier for the laity to understand.
As for the "eighty thousand dust-labors," this refers to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*); it is merely a general enumeration of their total number.
This refers to the ten fundamental afflictions: first, greed; second, hatred; third, pride; fourth, ignorance; fifth, doubt; sixth, wrong view; seventh, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
eighth, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); ninth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and tenth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Since each of these afflictions possesses further powers, they each constitute ten [sub-afflictions], making one hundred in total. These are further divided into three grades; the superior grade is classified as "superior" because it is heavy.
The intermediate and inferior grades together constitute three hundred; since the intermediate and inferior are not further subdivided, each becomes one hundred, totaling five hundred.

These five hundred arise collectively toward one's own five sense objects, and another five hundred arise collectively toward the five sense objects of others; these are called the original one thousand.
Furthermore, if one separately gives rise to five hundred for each of the five sense objects of both self and others, they become five thousand, based on distinct delusions.
Since each of the Four Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—has five thousand [aspects], they total twenty thousand; adding the original one thousand, they become twenty-one thousand.
Because these are multiplied by greed, hatred, delusion, and those who act with equal proportions of the three poisons, they become eighty-four thousand.
They are called "dust" (*rajas*) in the sense of defilement and "affliction" (*kleśa*) in the sense of agitation, as explained at length.
A separate explanation. △ Third, revealing the absence of self (anātman). Part one: General clarification.

one attains the fruit of Arhatship only when the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, at which point all sufferings are severed.

Foolish one, now that you know my fundamental emptiness, what use is there for greed, anger, killing, stealing, giving, or precepts?

(The note says: "To know the Truth of Suffering"—suffering takes the meaning of oppression, while *satya* [truth] is named for its function of revealing reality. The Buddha taught that suffering is definitively suffering; therefore, it is called the Truth of Suffering.)

It is said: "To know reality as it truly is" means to examine the meaning of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The essence of this Truth of Suffering is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of body and mind; because this body and mind are the basis upon which all suffering rests, they are called "all sufferings.

These "all sufferings" refer to the three sufferings, the four sufferings, the five sufferings, the eight sufferings, and so forth. The "three sufferings" are: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) regarding pleasant feelings, and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) regarding neutral feelings. The "four sufferings" are: birth, old age, sickness, and death. The "five sufferings" are the aforementioned four sufferings plus the suffering of the intense proliferation of the five aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

The "eight sufferings" are the aforementioned five sufferings plus the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hateful, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—these three added to the previous [three] make eight. Thus, one ultimately does not allow the mind to stagnate within the three realms and so forth.
This term is derived from its metaphorical meaning: just as a leaking house in the world is unfit for habitation and a leaking vessel is unfit for use, so too are the outflows (*āsrava*).

There are four kinds of outflows: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*).

Regarding "wholesome or unwholesome outflows of existence," this refers to the volition (*cetanā*) that acts as the basis [for rebirth], which simultaneously reigns over and is associated with the outflows; it pertains to the wholesome states and so forth that are cultivated.
All [of these] are subsumed under *sāsrava* (with-outflows), excluding *anāsrava* (without-outflows) wholesome states, as they are not the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

This severing of greed and the like still belongs to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Arising in succession, the wisdom that realizes the *tathatā* of self-emptiness has two functions.
First, it can sever delusions; second, it can realize the principle of the True Suchness of self-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*).

This refers to the principle of the emptiness of living beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is the aspect of the absence of a real, sovereign master within the five aggregates and so forth. It corresponds to the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) of the Hīnayāna:

first, the unconditioned phenomenon of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, the unconditioned phenomenon of non-deliberative cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, the unconditioned phenomenon of space (*ākāśa*). (The note states that these are called the Truth of Cessation [nirodha-satya]; "cessation" here refers to the exhaustion of burdens.)

When one attains [the realization of] "name," both delusion and suffering are extinguished, and the great afflictions are forever eradicated. The phrase "up to and including the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship" includes all intermediate stages.

However, within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the sequence of positions for severing and realizing [defilements] does not exceed the seven sages prior to the Path and the four fruits subsequent to the Path.

Regarding the seven sages: first is the contemplation of the five stabilizations (pañca-sthāpana-vipaśyanā), which refers to initially performing five types of contemplative visualization to bring the distracted mind to rest. First, the many...

1. Those with excessive greed practice the contemplation of impurity (the five types of impurity are: first, impurity of the seed; second, impurity of the dwelling place; third, impurity of the self-body; fourth, impurity of specific characteristics; and fifth, ultimate impurity). 2.
Those with excessive anger practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion. 3. Those with excessive delusion practice the contemplation of dependent origination.

4. Those with excessive distraction practice the contemplation of counting the breath. 2. The Contemplation of Specific Characteristics (observing the body and mind individually): [The practitioner] observes each aspect separately.

Regarding the mental factors (*cittadharma*): it means contemplating the impurity of the body (the five kinds of impurity as previously explained), contemplating that sensation is suffering (the suffering of pain, etc., also as previously explained), contemplating that the mind is impermanent (arising and ceasing moment by moment), and contemplating that phenomena are non-self (the provisional aggregation of the five aggregates). Because these four dharmas are observed individually and sequentially, they are called the "contemplation of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Third is the "contemplation of general characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*): this refers to the simultaneous application of the four contemplations—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—with respect to the body and so forth; because they occur at once, it is so named.
This is the mindfulness of general characteristics. These three preceding stages are called the four levels of the provisions (*sambhāra*). The first is the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*);

just as when drilling for fire, the initial sign of heat arises as a precursor to the actual fire, so too is the aspect of the Noble Path about to arise. This refers to the initial contemplation of the Four Truths of the Desire Realm, each having four aspects, totaling sixteen aspects.
Regarding the four aspects of Suffering: suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self. Regarding the four aspects of Origination: origination, cause, production, and condition.

Regarding the four aspects of cessation—namely, cessation, purity, excellence, and detachment—and the four aspects of the path—namely, the path, conformity, practice, and emergence—when these are combined with the Four Noble Truths for the two upper realms, there are sixteen aspects in each, totaling thirty-two.

Within this stage, one first gives rise to the contemplation of wisdom at the "Five Summits" (*mūrdhan*), which is the most supreme among the movable factors, just as the crown of a person's head is the most exalted. One also contemplates the preceding thirty [aspects].

Second, because the mind gradually matures through practice, there are the six stages of *kṣānti* (patience; they are called "patience" because one accepts the principles of the Truths). These *kṣāntis* are divided into three: the stage of lower *kṣānti*.

Within the thirty-two aspects [of the four truths], one confirms them; specifically, one performs seven cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana*) and twenty-four cycles of reducing the aspects (*ākāra*).
For example, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm through the aspect of impermanence, and so on, up to contemplating it through the aspect of conditioned origination (*saṃskāra*).
On the path of the higher realms, the stage of Supreme Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) lasts for only a single moment; it involves a renewed contemplation of the suffering of the desire realm.

The Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), being the foremost among the paths with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), also lasts for only a single moment; it likewise involves a renewed contemplation of the suffering of the desire realm.

These two stages differ from the preceding "Patience" (*kṣānti*) in terms of the superiority or inferiority of their wisdom (*jñāna*). (This above clarifies the seven types of noble persons prior to the Path. Regarding the four fruits following the Path, there are therein the four candidates (*pratipannaka*) and the four fruits (*phala*).

These are called the eight classes of persons. The first, those entering the stream (srotāpanna-pratipannaka), cultivate the sixteen moments of mind. This refers to each of the eight truths—four lower and four higher—having one patience (*kṣānti*) and one knowledge (*jñāna*).

For example, when taking the Four Truths of the Desire Realm as an object, there arises the patience for the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

The same applies to the three [subsequent truths] of origin, cessation, and the path. Regarding the Four Truths of the Higher Realms, they are termed "patience for subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*); this is because they are of the same kind as the suffering of the Desire Realm. Suffering...

Among these, the eight *kṣāntis* (patiences) of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and so forth are called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Regarding the preceding fifteen moments of mind, the eight paths of uninterrupted transition and seven paths of liberation are termed "stream-enterer-in-approach" (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*). The sixteenth moment of mind, the eighth path of liberation, is termed the "fruit of stream-entry" (*srotāpatti-phala*).

At this stage, there are two modes of activity: first, one is correctly abiding in the fruit; second, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) have not yet been severed.

All these belong to the fruit of the two types of progress on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Those belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) consist of the six uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and five paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for abandoning the sixth grade of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;

this is called the candidate for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-pṛthagjana*). The sixth path of liberation is called the fruit of once-returner (because one returns to the desire realm only one more time).

The three uninterrupted paths and two paths of liberation for abandoning the final three grades [of afflictions] are called the candidate for the third fruit, the non-returner (*anāgāmin-pṛthagjana*).
The liberation known as the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) is so called because one will no longer return to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It consists of the abandonment of seventy-two categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the two upper realms (since there are eight stages in the upper realms and nine categories of afflictions per stage, there are seventy-two categories).

The seventy-second uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and the seventy-first liberation path (*vimuktimārga*) are termed the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*). All preceding stages belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The seventy-second liberation path is termed arhatship (*arhattva*).
In the Han [tradition], those who have realized the fruit are called the *pañca-dharmakāya* (fivefold dharma-body) and belong to the stage of "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

In Sanskrit, they are called *arhat* or *araha*, which is translated here as "one who is worthy" (*yogya*). This term has three meanings: first, one is worthy because one has already eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*); second, one is worthy because one will not undergo further existence in a future body; and third, one is worthy because one is fit to receive the sublime offerings of devas and humans.

As for the expression "extinguishing the body like ashes": *The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Just as when wood is burned by fire, the ash remains, so too, when the body is consumed by the fire of wisdom, only the ash of the five aggregates remains. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "When the body is reduced to ash, the mind is extinguished; this is called 'nirvāṇa with remainder' (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). Thus, it is said that the physical form is incinerated and ceases to exist.
The Wise One [Zhi] says: "The primary great affliction is having a body; therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-existence.
That which precedes the exhaustion of the form is the possession of wisdom; therefore, one severs wisdom to merge into the void. Wisdom is afflicted by the body, and the body is exhausted by wisdom.
Thus they revolve upon the long road, wearying without end. This is why those of the Lesser Vehicle, having attained the four fruits, employ the fire of transformation."
By burning the body, both body and wisdom are extinguished as one enters the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) to experience the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti-sukha*).

According to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the stage of the *pratyekabuddha* should be listed here. As for why it is not explicitly explained [in this treatise]: it is because they share the same contemplation of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) as the preceding *śrāvakas*, and likewise sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to realize the fruit of "ashes and cessation" (*bhasma-ccheda-phala*); therefore, it is not mentioned separately. △ Third, the conclusion of the subject matter.
Fundamentally,
according to this school, the two dharmas of matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), along with greed, hatred, and delusion, constitute the basis of the physical body and the receptacle world;
there are no other distinct dharmas that serve as the basis for the past or the future.
The *Dàochào* states: "Although there are many interpretations regarding the fundamental basis of birth and death according to the Hīnayāna, three points will be briefly cited here:
first, some calculate it to be material and mental phenomena (*rūpa-citta*), as explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.

The Sautrāntika masters maintain that present material and mental phenomena serve as the causes for defilement and purity; their intention is that, just as the eighth consciousness in the Mahāyāna serves as the 'perfumable' (*bhāvyatā*), [so too do these phenomena]."

The sense that the three poisons act as causes is like the Mahāyāna because they are capable of perfuming; thus the Āgamas state that "lust, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world," and so forth.

When these three are taken together, they combine the two preceding meanings, which accord with the Mahāyāna in that only when there is both the capacity to perfume and the object perfumed does the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) flow on.
If this is so, how does it differ from the Mahāyāna? While it appears to reflect the intent of the Sūtras, it is not identical to them.
However, because only the six consciousnesses serve as the perfumed (bhāvyamāna) and not the eighth, even if one speaks of the ālayavijñāna, it exists only as a name;
furthermore, since the perfuming agent (bhāvaka) is also not the seventh consciousness, they are entirely different.

As for the statement regarding the past and future, this uses the present as an analogy for the other two time periods, taking matter-and-mind and the three poisons as the basis, without seeking any separate dharmas. △ Three.
Regarding that refutation, there are three parts; first is the heading.
Now, we shall refute it as follows:
△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts; first is the establishment of the principle.
Now, that which serves as the fundamental basis for the self throughout successive lifetimes must, by its very nature, be uninterrupted.

This is refuted through the meaning of the Mahāyāna: as for the claim that it must be uninterrupted by its very nature, this is because the Mahāyāna speaks of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*).
As the treatise states: "It perpetually revolves like a torrential stream," and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "From beginningless time..."
Since it is stated that the "dhātu is the universal support for all phenomena" and has existed from beginningless time, one knows that it is uninterrupted.
△ Next, the formal refutation:

Now, the five consciousnesses do not arise when their conditions (such as the sense organs and objects) are lacking; furthermore, the mental consciousness does not sometimes function [in states such as] fainting, deep sleep, or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In the heavens of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), including the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), these four great elements do not exist.
Regarding the statement that [consciousness] does not arise due to the deficiency of conditions:

this refers to the Mahāyāna teaching that eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions, ear-consciousness from eight conditions, and nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses from seven conditions. (The note states: "Root" refers to the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); "object" refers to the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). These two are cited briefly because the other conditions are omitted accordingly.)

If there is a single object of focus, consciousness cannot arise. What is called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna) refers specifically to the independent mental consciousness (*mukhya-manovijñāna*). [In the commentary, five states in which it does not function are cited: 1. Fainting (*mūrchā*) and sleep (*svapna*)—these two states are explained in reference to the lower realms (*adhobhūmi*). 2.

The two meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—these are explained in reference to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhūmi*). Regarding the attainment of non-conception, mental activity does not arise; this is the meditative state sought by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). As for the attainment of cessation, the preceding six and seventh consciousnesses do not arise at all, hence it is named "cessation.

This attainment is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding the sequence of these two attainments, one should first enter the attainment of non-conception. As for the "Heaven of Non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-deva*), this refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conception. It means that within this heaven, the sixth consciousness, along with its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*), [are absent].

Regarding the "places where [the senses] do not function"—these five stages are all places where the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not function. As for the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*) being devoid of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it means that these four heavens entirely lack coarse form (*rūpa*);
because they possess only the four aggregates (*skandha*)—namely, mind and mental factors—they receive the name "formless.

The first five consciousnesses and so forth are precisely "without mind," and this [realm] is precisely "without form. They [the opponents] reckon that matter and mind are the fundamental basis; since both are now absent, there is no basis.
Wherein lies the meaning? △ Third, the conclusion of the objection:
How can this body and world be maintained so that they do not cease from lifetime to lifetime?
If, as permitted in the Mahāyāna, there exists the principle of an eighth consciousness that maintains the seeds, then this difficulty does not arise. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
This reveals that they have not yet attained full understanding; thus, those who devote themselves exclusively to this teaching have likewise failed to investigate the origin of the person.

*An Explanation of the Treatise on the Original Person in the Avataṃsaka*, Scroll Lower, composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánjué, who lectures on the sūtras and śāstras at Dàkāiyuán Monastery in Chāng’ān. △ Third:
Explaining the Mahāyāna Teachings on Dharmalakṣaṇa (Characteristics of Phenomena). Part One: Stating the Title.
Regarding the teachings on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Three Great Vehicles (*mahāyāna*):

because they fully cultivate the two benefits (*dvaya-artha*), fully realize the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), and transport beings to the ultimate other shore of bodhi and nirvāṇa—distinguishing themselves from the preceding Lesser Vehicle—they are called "Great.
To extensively explain the names and numerical categories of all phenomena is termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Teaching on the Characteristics of Dharmas (Dharmalakṣaṇa-śāstra). △ Second, the exposition of their tenets, in two parts: first, the general presentation.
It is taught that all sentient beings have, from time immemorial, possessed by their very nature (*dharmatā*) eight kinds of consciousness.
The term "all" refers to the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). "Beginningless and naturally so" distinguishes this from the eighty thousand kalpas and other such views held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Regarding the eight consciousnesses: first, eye-consciousness; second, ear-consciousness; third, nose-consciousness; fourth, tongue-consciousness; fifth, body-consciousness; sixth, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

seventh, the *manas* consciousness (here translated as "mind," which constantly and critically deliberates); and eighth, the *ālaya-vijñāna*. (*Manas* means "mind. It is preeminent because it constantly and critically deliberates.

Because it is distinct from other consciousnesses, the *ālaya*—here translated as "store"—possesses three meanings: that which stores (*ālayana*), that which is stored (*ālīyate*), and that which is clung to as a self (*ātma-grāha*). △ Second, the specific explanation of the root and its branches has two parts;
first, the designation of the root.
Among these, the eighth, the ālayavijñāna, is their fundamental basis.

It is called "fundamental" because this consciousness maintains the seeds of the names and conventions of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and serves as the support for the seven transforming consciousnesses and their objects;
furthermore, it continues uninterruptedly from cause to fruit, and is therefore specifically termed "mind" (*citta*).
In Sanskrit, *citta* has the meaning of "accumulation" (*cita*), because it accumulates all seeds and gives rise to their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).

Taking the three categories of seeds, the physical body as the root, and the receptacle world as its objects, there are generally three states: 1. The state of being stored through the grasping of self-love (*ātmasneha-ālaya*);

the meaning of the name is as explained previously. 2. The state of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma; in Sanskrit this is called *vipāka*, which here means "maturation" (*yìshú*). It exists.

It receives the name "ripening" (*vipāka*) for three reasons: first, it ripens at a different time—karma created in the past is experienced as retribution in the present life, and karma created in the present life is experienced in a future life;
second, it ripens through transformation—because the cause perishes when the fruit arises;

third, it ripens as a different category—because the cause comprises both the wholesome and the unwholesome, whereas the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, it maintains the continuity of the stream of existence.

The term *ālaya* in Sanskrit is translated here as "holding" (*ādāna*), meaning that from the stage of an ordinary being until the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it holds both the profane and the sacred.
Although it transforms into the Perfect Mirror Wisdom within the state of fruition, it is merely a transformation of name and not a transformation of essence.
Because it possesses these many meanings, it can serve as the fundamental basis. △ Second, explaining why it constitutes the fundamental basis.

The seeds of the root-body (*mūla-kāya*) and the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*) undergo instantaneous transformation, giving rise to the seven consciousnesses, all of which are capable of manifesting their respective objects;
yet, none of these possess any real dharmas.

The phrase "instantaneous transformation of the resultant body and so forth" explains the meaning of being established as the basis; the "capable transformer" (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) is precisely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

That which is transformed consists of the two divisions of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiver (darśana-bhāga); therefore, it is established as *vijñapti-mātra*. As for "transformation," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* quotes the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, stating that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as these two divisions;

both the perceived and the perceiver arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). Based on these two divisions, the designations of self and phenomena are established, for those two have no basis apart from this.
Regarding the statement that the seven consciousnesses are produced through transformation, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* cites the *Laṅkāvatāra*: [text continues].

For example, just as the great waves of the ocean arise from the fierce winds, and the surging billows toss upon the vast abyss without ceasing for a moment, so too is it with the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Stirred by the winds of objective conditions, the various waves of consciousness leap forth and arise in succession.
Therefore, one should know that the seven consciousnesses are all produced through the transformation of the *ālaya*, and that they are all capable of manifesting [their objects].

"Those which are one's own objects of cognition" refers to the seven consciousnesses, each of which possesses the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), both of which arise from their respective self-cognitions (*svasaṃvitti*).

Therefore, the statement that "there are no real dharmas whatsoever" is intended to negate a real self or dharmas existing apart from consciousness. △ Third, the interrogation and explanation, in two parts:
first, the interrogation.
"How does it transform?

This inquiry is posed by the opponent because, upon first hearing the doctrine of the transformation of consciousness, they have not yet grasped its underlying meaning. △ Second, the explanation of the four [aspects] begins with the primary explanation.

This means that due to the power of the habitual perfuming of the discrimination between self and dharmas, when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as if they were a self and dharmas;
because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are shrouded by ignorance, they take these appearances as objects and grasp them as a real self and real dharmas.

All of this refers to what that treatise calls the "discrimination of self and dharmas": sentient beings, from beginningless time, have erroneously conceptualized various discriminations of self and dharmas through the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which then perfume the *ālayavijñāna* to form seeds.

When the *ālayavijñāna* gives rise to the seven consciousnesses, each of these seven consciousnesses possesses both a transforming subject (*pariṇāma*) and a transformed object (*pariṇāmita*). Those transformed objects appear as real selves and dharmas.
The sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] do not understand and grasp what is merely apparent as being real. The reason they do not understand is that they are shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*).

For example, it is like a craftsman who fashions a ghost at the gate of a temple; later, when passing by, he becomes deluded and intoxicated, mistakenly perceiving it as a real ghost and giving rise to fear, unaware that it was originally his own creation.
In this way, ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), deluded and ignorant, grasp at a real self (*ātman*).
The Dharma is not known to be what is manifested by one's own consciousness through its own habitual perfuming; it is likewise with this [ignorance].
As for why other consciousnesses are not mentioned, it is because the first five and the eighth lack this grasping.

That which takes this grasping as a real self and phenomena refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which engage in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), just as one might grasp at empty flowers or two moons as being real flowers and real moons.
...and so forth. △ Second, the illustration through analogy, which has two parts. First, the presentation of the two analogies:

(1) As in the case of one suffering from a grave illness whose mind is clouded and who perceives strange colors, people, and objects; (2) as in the case of a dreamer, who, due to the power of dreaming, perceives various external objective phenomena appearing before the mind.
In this context, the word "this" (ci) refers to the person and is not a citation of the preceding statement. The "affliction" and the "dream" are two metaphors;
either one of these two is capable of producing false perception, which is easy to understand.

Regarding the statement that "the mind appears as various external objective phenomena," what is seen in a dream—the sense organs, the body, and the physical world—is entirely a transformation of the mind; apart from the mind, there are no separate sense organs.
Because it is the realm of the body-vessel. △ Second, citing dreams as appropriate to the context: first, the analogy for when ordinary beings are deluded;
during a dream, they grasp at external objects as being truly existent.
△ Second, the analogy for when noble ones have attained realization.
Upon waking, one finally realizes that it was merely a transformation of a dream.

The two metaphors above have been presented; here below, for the sake of convenience, only the dream is cited. The metaphor above illustrates how ordinary beings, while deluded, only realize [the truth] upon waking;
the metaphor below illustrates how the various sages understand the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). △ Third, the application to the Dharma, in two parts: first—
In summary: my own body is likewise a transformation of consciousness alone.

One should state that the sense organs, the body, and the environment are likewise so; however, the text is abbreviated for stylistic reasons. △ Second, the specific application of the analogy, which has two parts. First, the application.

At the time of dreaming, because of delusion, one clings to the existence of a self and various objects; from this, afflictions arise and karma is created, leading to an endless cycle of birth and death (as explained in detail previously).
△ Subsequently, upon waking from sleep:
Only upon awakening to this principle does one realize that one’s own body is a transformation of consciousness alone.
Due to delusion, one clings to its existence—as previously mentioned regarding the time of dreaming and so forth—from which afflictions arise (and so forth).
This is like a person in a dream who clings to the dream-objects as being truly existent; consequently, within the dream, they may experience grief or joy, and undergo suffering.

Regarding the various distinct characteristics of the experience of pleasure (the note states that "as explained extensively before" refers to the causes and effects of good and evil as taught for humans, devas, and the Hīnayāna;

from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, these are all transformations of consciousness. The previous school did not understand this and took them to be truly existent; if one explains their mode of activity (*ākāra*), it is no different from that [Mahāyāna view]). To realize and understand this principle corresponds to the preceding passage beginning with "having awakened.

Regarding the phrase "transformed by consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra-pariṇata*): "only" (*mātra*) has the sense of exclusion and maintenance; it excludes that which exists outside of consciousness.

The dharmas apprehended by consciousness that are transformed [by it] are not entirely non-existent; furthermore, "only" (*kevala*) has the sense of determination, meaning that there is determinately only the transforming consciousness.

Moreover, "only" indicates prominence; it does not mean that mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth are absent, but because consciousness is predominant, the "king" (the primary factor) is mentioned to include its "retainers" (the mental factors).
Thus, one speaks simply of "consciousness," for consciousness has the function of discerning (*vijñapti*).
The eight [consciousnesses] all perform discernment (*vijñapti*), as explained at length in that treatise. △ Fourth, the conclusion establishing the basis of what is perceived:
consciousness is the basis of the body (the meaning of "non-discernment" will be refuted later).
The Formation of the Fundamental [Critique] (Note: This can be understood from the subsequent refutation).

△ Second, the explanation.
